question: A media analytics company is building a RAG assistant on AWS by using Amazon Bedrock for text generation. For the retrieval layer, some workloads use Amazon OpenSearch Service for vector search, while other workloads use Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension for advanced metadata filtering. The GenAI team wants a single, consistent retrieval interface that Bedrock-based applications can use without being rewritten when the underlying vector store changes. Which solution will provide the MOST seamless integration mechanism for retrieval augmentation across these vector stores?
options: A) Create two Amazon API Gateway endpoints: one backed by an AWS Lambda function that queries OpenSearch and another backed by a different Lambda function that queries Aurora. Instruct the foundation model in the prompt to call the appropriate endpoint based on the user's request.

B) Implement separate retrieval modules in the application code: one that queries OpenSearch using its vector search APIs and another that queries Aurora using SQL with pgvector. Add conditional logic in each application to select the correct module.

C) Create a stateless Model Context Protocol (MCP) server (for example, on AWS Lambda) that exposes a single tool such as "vector_search" with a stable JSON input/output contract. Use an MCP client library in the application/agent runtime to call this tool, and route the request internally to OpenSearch or Aurora as needed.

D) Store embeddings and document chunks directly in Amazon S3 objects and retrieve relevant chunks by using S3 prefix filters and object metadata filters. Pass the retrieved objects as context to the model.
explanation: A stable tool-like contract in front of the retrieval layer is what decouples FM-integrated apps from the underlying vector store. An MCP server exposing one "vector_search" tool with a fixed JSON contract lets the backend swap between OpenSearch and Aurora/pgvector internally with zero change to how the app/agent invokes retrieval. A) Prompt-based endpoint selection is brittle — routing correctness depends on the model reliably picking the right endpoint, and access patterns still differ per store. B) Conditional application-level modules duplicate integration logic and force code changes/redeploys whenever the vector store choice changes — the opposite of a consistent interface. D) S3 prefix/metadata filtering is not semantic (kNN) search at all — it fails the core requirement of vector retrieval, regardless of consistency.
domain: Domain 1 — Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
task: 1.5 — Design retrieval mechanisms for FM augmentation

question: A SaaS provider is building a customer-support chat application that uses the Amazon Bedrock Converse API with a single FM. The application stores full conversation history in Amazon DynamoDB and uses an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base for RAG. As usage grows, the company's Bedrock spend increases sharply, and some requests fail when the prompt exceeds the model's context window. The company wants to reduce token-related costs while preserving answer quality. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: A) Increase the knowledge base chunk size so that fewer chunks are retrieved, and disable metadata-based filtering to avoid excluding potentially relevant content. Send the larger chunks to the FM to preserve answer quality.

B) Implement prompt compression by using a smaller FM to summarize older conversation history into a short running summary that is stored in DynamoDB. Include only the summary plus the most recent turns in each request and set maxTokens to limit response size.

C) Enable Amazon Bedrock provisioned throughput and use the latency-optimized performance configuration for the FM to reduce per-request token costs and prevent context-window overflow errors during peak traffic.

D) Before each model invocation, call the Amazon Bedrock CountTokens API to estimate total input size. If the request exceeds a token budget, prune older conversation turns and reduce the number of retrieved chunks from the knowledge base. Publish input and output token counts to Amazon CloudWatch for ongoing tracking.

E) Enable Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the application's system prompt and few-shot examples so the cached prefix is discounted. Keep the full conversation history and the same number of retrieved RAG chunks in every request.
explanation: Real token-cost reduction requires cutting how many tokens actually enter the request, not just changing throughput/latency settings or caching a static prefix. B) Summarizing older turns into a compact running summary plus recent turns directly shrinks input tokens while retaining key context; maxTokens bounds output cost. D) CountTokens gives a pre-invocation size estimate so the app can enforce a token budget by pruning history and trimming retrieved chunks — a deterministic, measurable control loop (reinforced by CloudWatch tracking). A) is wrong — larger chunks raise, not lower, tokens per retrieval, and disabling metadata filtering adds noise. C) is wrong — provisioned throughput/latency-optimized configs affect speed and per-request cost curve, not prompt size, so they don't fix context-window overflow. E) is wrong — caching discounts a repeated static prefix but does nothing to the dynamic (and here, unreduced) conversation history and RAG context, so overflow risk and dynamic-token spend remain.
domain: Domain 4 — Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
task: 4.1 — Implement cost optimization and resource efficiency strategies

question: A media company is building an internal "chat with your documents" assistant by using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases backed by Amazon OpenSearch Service. Source documents are stored in Amazon S3 and include multiple versions of policies written by different teams. Users frequently ask questions such as "What is the latest policy for content takedown?" and need the response to reflect the correct business unit and the most recent document. The company wants to improve retrieval precision and give the FM better context (for example, document timestamps and authorship) with the LEAST operational overhead. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: A) Build a custom post-processing Lambda function that invokes an FM to extract author and timestamp from each retrieved chunk at query time and then reranks the results before sending them to the user.
B) Increase the chunk size and overlap settings so each chunk contains the document cover page that lists the author and publication date, ensuring the FM always receives this context in the prompt.
C) Regenerate embeddings with a larger vector dimensionality for the embedding model so the vector store can better distinguish older and newer versions of similar documents.

D) Define a standardized metadata schema (for example, business_unit, author, document_timestamp, topic tags). Store timestamps and authorship as S3 object metadata or as extracted fields, and configure the knowledge base to treat these fields as metadata (not content) so retrieval can use them to improve ranking and context.
explanation: Explicit, structured metadata (business_unit, author, document_timestamp, tags) kept separate from chunk content is the lowest-overhead way to give retrieval a reliable signal for versioning/ownership, and gives the FM grounding context without polluting the embedding text. D) sets this up once at ingestion and lets the knowledge base use it consistently for ranking and filtering. A) adds a per-query FM call plus custom rerank logic — real-time cost and complexity for something metadata already solves at ingestion. B) stuffs cover-page text into chunk content, increasing tokens and noise while making metadata fragile to chunk boundaries. C) bigger embedding dimensionality raises storage/compute cost but doesn't encode version/ownership semantics — that's a structured-data problem, not a semantic-similarity problem.

question: A large enterprise stores millions of documents that are used to ground responses generated by a foundation model. Users frequently ask time bound and ownership specific questions such as retrieving the most recent policy written by a particular team or documents approved within a specific quarter. The current retrieval approach scans content extensively and struggles to return results quickly as the dataset continues to grow. The engineering team wants to improve search precision and latency by redesigning how documents are described and filtered before being passed to the model. The solution must scale to millions of objects, support fast filtering on attributes like timestamps and authorship. As a GenAI developer, how would you design the MOST efficient metadata framework to meet these requirements?
options: A) Generate vector embeddings for all documents and encode timestamps and authorship into the embedding input. Store embeddings in a vector database and retrieve documents using similarity search only. Use prompt logic to infer metadata relevance instead of explicit filtering.

B) Store document attributes inside the document body and rely on full text search to extract timestamps and authorship during retrieval. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service keyword queries to scan document content across the repository. Increase shard count and replica settings to handle scale.

C) Store document attributes such as creation date, author, and domain as Amazon S3 object metadata and object tags at upload time. Use S3 Metadata, which introduces live inventory tables that work with familiar SQL based tools, to query these attributes efficiently at scale. Filter matching objects using SQL queries before retrieving content for foundation model context.

D) Store document attributes as Amazon S3 object metadata and object tags, and additionally generate embeddings for each document to support semantic ranking across the dataset. Index both metadata and embeddings in Amazon OpenSearch Service and rerank results before sending them to the model. Maintain periodic re indexing workflows to keep vector representations synchronized with metadata updates.
explanation: Time-bound and ownership-specific questions are answerable with deterministic structured-attribute filtering — semantic similarity search isn't the right tool at all, so the most efficient design skips embeddings entirely. C) Storing creation date, author, and domain as S3 object metadata/tags at upload time, then using S3 Metadata's live inventory tables with familiar SQL queries, filters matching objects fast and deterministically at millions-of-objects scale, entirely independent of document content — only relevant objects are retrieved for FM context, with no embedding pipeline to build or maintain. A) Encoding timestamps/authorship into embeddings and relying on similarity search alone is imprecise for exact date/ownership filtering, reduces interpretability, and adds significant compute/storage cost for a problem that's fundamentally structured-attribute filtering, not semantic matching. B) Embedding attributes in document content and full-text-scanning to extract them doesn't scale efficiently for large object counts and isn't optimized for structured attribute extraction — more shards improves throughput but doesn't reduce the fundamental query inefficiency. D) Adding embeddings and OpenSearch indexing/reranking on top of the correct metadata approach is unnecessary cost and complexity (embedding generation, periodic reindexing) for queries explicitly driven by structured attributes, not semantic ranking.
domain: Domain 1 — Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
task: 1.4 — Design and implement vector store solutions
comparison_note: Escalates AIPC01_D1_002's lesson (store structured attributes like business_unit/author/timestamp as S3 object metadata, NOT embedded in chunk content, for precision retrieval in a Bedrock Knowledge Base) with the newer S3 Metadata feature: live, SQL-queryable inventory tables purpose-built for fast attribute filtering at millions-of-objects scale. Same core principle in both — keep structured attributes OUT of embeddings/content and query them directly — this question just names the specific scaled-up mechanism (S3 Metadata inventory tables + SQL) for very large corpora.

question: A platform team at a regulated financial institution is building multiple internal applications that invoke Amazon Bedrock FMs for tasks such as summarization and drafting customer communications. The team must ensure that all applications use consistent, centrally managed prompts. Prompt changes must be reviewed and approved before they can be used in production, and auditors must be able to determine who used which prompt version and when. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: A) Create an Amazon API Gateway front end that injects a standard system prompt by using request mapping templates. Enable AWS WAF to block prompt injection attempts and use access logs in API Gateway for auditing.

B) Store prompt templates as AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store parameters and inject them into AWS Lambda environment variables during deployment. Enable Amazon CloudWatch metrics for token usage to track prompt usage over time.

C) Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to create reusable, parameterized prompts with versioning and an approval workflow. Store the prompt template repository in Amazon S3 as the source of truth. Enable AWS CloudTrail to audit Bedrock API usage and send application prompt/response access logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

D) Use Amazon SageMaker Model Registry to store and approve prompt templates as model package versions. Enable Amazon CloudWatch Logs for SageMaker endpoint invocation logging and use AWS CloudTrail for auditing.
explanation: The requirement is a full prompt lifecycle: centralized reusable templates, versioning, approval before production use, and a who/what/when audit trail. C) Bedrock Prompt Management is purpose-built for exactly this — parameterized templates, version control, and approval promotion — while CloudTrail supplies the authoritative API-call audit record and CloudWatch Logs centralizes prompt/response access logging across apps. A) API Gateway mapping templates can inject a fixed prompt fragment but has no versioning/approval concept; WAF addresses injection security, not governance; API Gateway logs show API traffic, not prompt-version usage. B) Parameter Store + Lambda env vars distributes text but leaves versioning, approval workflow, and per-invocation audit to be custom-built per app — high overhead. D) SageMaker Model Registry governs model package versions, not Bedrock prompt templates — it's the wrong tool for where prompts are actually consumed, adding unnecessary components.
domain: Domain 1 — Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
task: 1.6 — Implement prompt engineering strategies and governance for FM interactions
comparison_note: Compare with AIPC01_D1_009: both pick Bedrock Prompt Management as (part of) the correct answer, but for different requirement emphases. This question's (D1_003) driver is prompt LIFECYCLE GOVERNANCE — versioning, an approval workflow before production use, and a who-used-which-version-and-when audit trail — so the correct combo adds S3 (repository) + CloudTrail (API audit) + CloudWatch Logs (access logging). D1_009's driver is BEHAVIORAL CONSISTENCY + OUTPUT SAFETY across apps — the same role/JSON-schema template reused everywhere, paired with Guardrails topic filtering and PII masking, with no approval-workflow or audit-trail requirement. Read for the requirement keyword: 'approved before production' + 'who used which version and when' → Prompt Management + CloudTrail/CloudWatch audit stack; 'consistent behavior across apps' + 'fixed JSON output' + 'prevent PII/restricted topics' → Prompt Management + Guardrails. Also see AIPC01_D1_023 — a near-duplicate of this same prompt-governance pattern (Prompt Management + versioned S3 repo + manual approval + CloudTrail + CloudWatch Logs) reused with a different industry framing and different wrong-answer distractors.

question: A financial market data provider's AI platform team manages Amazon Bedrock prompts that are used by multiple internal applications. Developers currently copy prompt text into application repositories, which has caused inconsistent behavior and unclear ownership of production changes. The team needs reusable parameterized templates, controlled promotion of prompt changes, a stable versioned production reference for each approved prompt, auditability for prompt resource changes, and application-emitted access logs for troubleshooting. Which approach will meet these requirements with the MOST appropriate governance?
options: A) Store each prompt template in AWS Secrets Manager with a separate secret for each environment. Rotate prompt secrets after approval, audit secret updates with CloudTrail, and emit application access metadata to CloudWatch Logs.

B) Create prompts in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management with variables and versions. Store prompt source artifacts in a versioned S3 repository. Promote prompt versions through a manual deployment approval step, audit Bedrock API activity with CloudTrail, and write prompt access metadata from applications to CloudWatch Logs.

C) Define each prompt as an Amazon Bedrock Flow node with input variables. Store the Flow JSON definitions in S3. Promote Flow aliases after review, audit Flow API calls with CloudTrail, and emit orchestration logs to CloudWatch Logs.

D) Store prompt templates as encrypted S3 objects with object tags for environments. Load the latest approved object at application startup. Track S3 object reads with CloudTrail data events, and emit application request metadata to CloudWatch Logs.
explanation: Reusable parameterized templates, controlled promotion, a stable versioned production reference, resource-change auditability, and app-emitted access logs map directly onto Bedrock's native prompt governance resource plus standard audit/logging services. B) Bedrock Prompt Management provides variables and versions as first-class features — a stable snapshot each app references instead of copying raw text; a versioned S3 repository holds source artifacts; a manual approval step controls promotion; CloudTrail audits Bedrock API activity (resource changes); CloudWatch Logs captures app-emitted access metadata for troubleshooting — full coverage, no custom template system to build. A) Secrets Manager is built for credentials/sensitive config, not governed content artifacts — rotation isn't an appropriate promotion model for prompt text, and it provides no Bedrock-native versioned production reference. C) Bedrock Flows orchestrate multi-step workflows — using a Flow as the primary container for every reusable prompt adds unnecessary orchestration overhead when the actual need is centralized prompt template governance, which Prompt Management addresses more directly. D) S3-only storage with object tags provides storage/object-level history but no Bedrock prompt resource or managed version reference — applications still need custom template loading, parameter handling, and validation logic, increasing drift risk across teams.

question: A fintech support engineering team is building a customer chat assistant by using an FM in Amazon Bedrock. The assistant must consistently behave like a regulated customer support agent across multiple applications, must return responses in a fixed JSON structure that downstream systems can parse, and must prevent the FM from returning personally identifiable information (PII) or discussing restricted topics. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: A) Fine-tune a Bedrock custom model on company support transcripts that always follow the JSON format and never includes PII. Deploy the fine-tuned model and remove all prompt instructions to reduce token usage.

B) Store prompt text templates in an Amazon S3 bucket and have each application load and assemble prompts at runtime. Use AWS Lambda to call Amazon Comprehend for PII detection and redaction before and after each model invocation.

C) Create a reusable, parameterized prompt template in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management that defines the agent role and includes explicit JSON output instructions (schema and example). Attach Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with topic filtering and PII masking, and invoke the managed prompt from all applications.

D) Configure Amazon API Gateway request validation with a JSON Schema model and reject any Bedrock request that does not include the required output fields. Rely on the FM to comply with the schema and avoid restricted topics.
explanation: Consistent cross-application agent behavior, enforced structured output, and content restriction (PII/topics) is a combination of centralized prompt reuse plus managed safety filtering. C) A Bedrock Prompt Management template centralizes the role definition and JSON schema/example so every application invokes the identical governed prompt; Guardrails topic filtering + PII masking handle content restriction at the model boundary — both managed, minimal custom code. A) Fine-tuning is high-effort/cost and, critically, removing prompt instructions strips away the controllability that keeps behavior consistent and governable — the opposite of what's needed. B) S3-stored templates plus custom Lambda/Comprehend pre/post-processing duplicates governance logic per application and adds real operational surface compared to one centralized managed prompt + guardrail. D) API Gateway request validation checks incoming API requests, not the FM's generated output — it cannot enforce JSON structure or content safety on what the model actually produces.

question: A regional pharmacy benefits manager's clinical AI team is standardizing an Amazon Bedrock assistant that drafts prior authorization summaries. Three internal applications will call the same chat model by using the Converse API. The team must centralize reusable role instructions, support runtime substitution of case details, keep JSON formatting guidance consistent across applications, maintain prompt versions for controlled rollout, and enforce responsible AI controls outside the prompt text. Which implementation will meet these requirements with the LEAST duplication?
options: A) Create a versioned chat prompt in Prompt Management with system instructions, messages that use {{caseSummary}} variables, and JSON formatting instructions. Invoke the prompt ARN with Converse, and override inferenceConfig and additionalModelRequestFields per application.

B) Create a versioned chat prompt in Prompt Management with system instructions, messages that define 25 inputVariables for all policy fields and response sections, and JSON formatting instructions. Invoke the prompt ARN with Converse, and enforce safety with a separate Guardrail.

C) Create a versioned managed prompt in Prompt Management with both chat and text PromptTemplateConfiguration sections, and select the needed template in each request. Invoke the prompt ARN with Converse by passing promptVariables, and enforce safety with a separate Guardrail.

D) Create a versioned chat prompt in Prompt Management with system instructions, messages that use {{caseSummary}} variables, and JSON formatting instructions. Invoke the prompt ARN with Converse by passing promptVariables, and enforce safety with a separate Bedrock Guardrail.
explanation: Centralized reusable instructions, runtime variable substitution, versioned controlled rollout, and responsible AI enforcement kept OUT of the prompt text all map to Prompt Management's chat prompt features used correctly, plus a separate Guardrail. D) A versioned chat prompt with {{caseSummary}}-style variables and JSON formatting guidance centralizes the instruction framework; passing promptVariables at Converse invocation supplies runtime case details correctly; a separate Bedrock Guardrail enforces safety independent of prompt wording — exactly the documented, least-duplication pattern. A) When invoking a Prompt Management prompt by ARN with Converse, fields like inferenceConfig and additionalModelRequestFields should NOT be included in the request — this option misuses the managed-prompt invocation pattern. B) 25 inputVariables exceeds the documented maximum of 20 for a chat prompt template — this configuration is invalid as designed and needs consolidation. C) PromptTemplateConfiguration is a union — a single managed prompt template configuration can specify only chat OR text, not both — trying to combine them doesn't match the documented API structure.

task: 1.6 — Implement prompt engineering strategies and governance for FM interactions

This question tests the exact API mechanics underneath that same pattern: the {{variable}} syntax and promptVariables invocation parameter, the documented 20-inputVariables limit for chat prompt templates, the PromptTemplateConfiguration union constraint (chat OR text, never both), and the rule that inferenceConfig/additionalModelRequestFields must NOT be set when invoking a managed prompt by ARN. Same underlying governance philosophy as D1_009 and the D1_003/D1_023 prompt-governance pair, tested at a much finer technical grain.

question: A team is developing a generative AI assistant that produces multi step analytical responses, such as reasoning through policy eligibility, summarizing complex documents, and explaining recommendations to internal reviewers. Early testing shows that while the model answers are generally correct, the reasoning is often shallow, inconsistent, or difficult to follow, especially for complex inputs that require intermediate steps and structured thinking. The team wants to improve response quality without fine tuning the foundation model. They want an approach that systematically improves reasoning clarity, enforces predictable output structure, and allows the team to iteratively refine prompts using feedback and evaluation signals over time. What do you recommend?
options: A) Use Amazon Bedrock with few shot examples that demonstrate the final answer format but suppress intermediate reasoning steps. Invoke the model through AWS Lambda and leverage repeated inference calls to improve consistency. Measure success by evaluating final answer accuracy.

B) Use Amazon Bedrock to fine tune a custom model with curated reasoning datasets and deploy it behind an endpoint. Trigger retraining pipelines using AWS Step Functions whenever output quality degrades. Leverage model retraining to improve reasoning.

C) Use Amazon Bedrock with a zero shot prompt that asks the model to provide a concise answer only, while enforcing a JSON output schema. Invoke the model from AWS Lambda and validate responses using schema checks in application code. Prioritize model output validation over model reasoning to improve response quality.

D) Use Amazon Bedrock with zero shot chain of thought prompting by explicitly instructing the model to reason step by step and produce a structured output format. Invoke the model from AWS Lambda and log intermediate responses to Amazon CloudWatch for prompt evaluation and iterative refinement. Use prompt versioning to continuously improve reasoning quality without retraining the model.
explanation: Deeper, more consistent reasoning without retraining comes from explicitly instructing the model to reason step by step, combined with logging and versioning that let engineers actually observe and iterate on how reasoning quality changes. D) Zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting explicitly asks the model to articulate intermediate reasoning before the final answer, directly improving coherence and depth for complex analytical tasks; logging intermediate responses to CloudWatch gives visibility into HOW reasoning evolves across prompt versions, enabling a genuine iterative refinement loop — all without touching the model itself. A) Few-shot examples that SUPPRESS intermediate reasoning steps directly work against improving reasoning depth, and evaluating only final-answer accuracy hides reasoning failures — repeated inference calls don't create a systematic feedback loop for prompt design either. B) Fine-tuning is exactly the model-retraining path the requirement explicitly wants to avoid — higher cost, longer iteration cycles, more operational complexity, and it shifts focus away from the faster, more flexible prompt-engineering techniques the team wants to use. C) A concise-answer-only instruction plus schema validation improves output STRUCTURE and consistency but does nothing for the model's internal REASONING process — prioritizing validation over reasoning misses the core requirement to improve analytical depth and clarity.
domain: Domain 1 — Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
task: 1.6 — Implement prompt engineering strategies and governance for FM interactions
comparison_note: Different layer of prompt work than AIPC01_D1_003/AIPC01_D1_023/AIPC01_D1_009/AIPC01_D1_033. Those questions are about prompt GOVERNANCE infrastructure — centralized reusable templates, approval workflows, versioned production references, audit trails via Prompt Management + S3 + CloudTrail + CloudWatch. This question is about prompt CONTENT TECHNIQUE — chain-of-thought instruction specifically for improving reasoning depth and clarity, with 'prompt versioning' mentioned only as the lightweight mechanism for iterating on technique quality over time, not as a formal approval/promotion process. If the question is about WHO can change prompts and HOW changes get approved/audited → the governance family; if it's about WHAT to put in the prompt to make the model reason better → this chain-of-thought pattern.

question: A company operates a generative AI system that produces written recommendations used by different internal teams. During review cycles, stakeholders notice that certain phrasing patterns and contextual cues in the inputs and outputs can unintentionally influence how recommendations are framed. The team wants to introduce systematic controls so that inputs are normalized before inference and outputs are consistently adjusted before being consumed by downstream systems. The team also wants to automate comparisons without embedding complex logic directly into application code. The solution must support controlled experimentation, allow teams to compare different prompt handling strategies, and ensure that any pre processing and post processing steps are applied uniformly across evaluations. What do you recommend?
options: A) Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to version prompts and manually apply input normalization and output rewriting inside the prompt text. Switch prompt versions during testing to compare results across groups. Log outputs externally for later fairness analysis.

B) Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to maintain multiple prompt versions, attach metadata for fairness experiments, and leverage downstream systems to interpret and adjust outputs. Coordinate evaluations by switching prompts and correlating results manually across test runs.

C) Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows to orchestrate model calls, but embed all pre processing and post processing logic inside application code before invoking the flow. Use the flow to route requests and capture outputs. Compare results by toggling code paths during tests.

D) Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows to define a multi step workflow that applies standardized pre processing to inputs and post processing to outputs. Run A/B evaluations by comparing different flow variants and capture metrics automatically. Use the flow structure to ensure consistent handling across all evaluations.
explanation: Uniform pre/post-processing applied identically across every evaluation, without embedding transformation logic in application code, is exactly what a declarative multi-step orchestration tool provides — Prompt Management alone doesn't orchestrate steps, it just versions text. D) Prompt Flows define explicit orchestrated stages — standardized input normalization BEFORE inference and standardized output adjustment AFTER generation — applied consistently by the flow structure itself; comparing different FLOW VARIANTS (not code paths) makes the flow the unit of experimentation, with metrics captured automatically and uniform handling guaranteed across every evaluation run. A) Prompt Management versions prompt TEXT — manually baking normalization/rewriting INTO the prompt text makes behavior harder to reason about and inconsistent across evaluations, and manual comparison introduces analysis bias; there's no structured mechanism enforcing uniform pre/post steps. B) Prompt Management supports lifecycle versioning but doesn't enforce EXECUTION ORDER or transformation steps — relying on downstream systems to interpret/adjust outputs introduces variability outside the evaluation framework, and manual result correlation is error-prone. C) Even with Prompt Flows in use, pushing pre/post-processing logic into APPLICATION CODE (rather than the flow itself) splits responsibility across layers, undermines the flow's purpose of centralized declarative consistency, and makes experimentation harder to audit — toggling code paths is less transparent and repeatable than comparing flow variants.
domain: Domain 1 — Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
task: 1.6 — Implement prompt engineering strategies and governance for FM interactions
comparison_note: Marks the boundary of Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management, established across AIPC01_D1_003/D1_009/D1_023/D1_033: Prompt Management is for VERSIONING and REUSING a single prompt template with variables, approval, and audit trail — it does not orchestrate a multi-step pipeline of pre-processing → inference → post-processing, and it doesn't enforce execution order across steps. When the requirement is standardized, ORCHESTRATED transformation stages applied uniformly across A/B-comparable variants (as here), the correct tool is Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows, a different Bedrock capability from Prompt Management. If the question is about a single reusable prompt's lifecycle (versions, approval, audit) → Prompt Management (D1_003/D1_009/D1_023/D1_033 family); if it's about a multi-stage input→output PIPELINE with declarative pre/post-processing → Prompt Flows (this pattern).

question: An online retailer is building a customer-facing chat experience that uses Amazon Bedrock LLMs. The team wants to route each user message to a low-latency model for simple requests and to a higher-quality model for complex requests. During traffic spikes, the higher-quality model occasionally experiences throttling, and the team wants requests to automatically fall back to the low-latency model when throttling or high latency is detected. The team also wants a clear audit trail of how each request was routed. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom application logic?
options: A) Use Amazon API Gateway to invoke an AWS Step Functions state machine. In the state machine, run a classification step to determine request complexity, then use Choice states to route to the appropriate Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel task. Add retry logic and a fallback branch that routes to the low-latency model when throttling or latency thresholds are exceeded, and store routing outcomes in the execution history.

B) Enable Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference and create an inference profile so Bedrock automatically distributes requests. Use a single modelId in the application and rely on the inference profile to handle both complexity-based model selection and throttling fallback.

C) Implement all routing in application code inside a single AWS Lambda function. The function calls Amazon Bedrock, checks for throttling errors, retries with exponential backoff, and then calls a different model if throttling persists. Log routing decisions to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

D) Create two Amazon API Gateway endpoints (for example, /fast and /accurate). Configure the client application to call the appropriate endpoint based on request complexity. Use separate AWS Lambda integrations to invoke the corresponding Bedrock model.
explanation: The task needs two decision layers — content-based routing (simple vs complex) and operational fallback (throttling/latency) — plus a built-in audit trail, all with minimal custom code. A) Step Functions is managed orchestration purpose-built for this: Choice states handle branching, native retry/fallback handles throttling, and execution history is the audit trail for free. B) Cross-Region inference profiles solve regional capacity distribution, not content-based routing across different models, and give no auditable routing decision record. C) A single Lambda can technically do it, but every piece — branching, retries, fallback, audit logging — has to be hand-built and is less structured/traceable than orchestration state. D) Two static endpoints push the routing decision to the client, so there's no automatic fallback on throttling/latency and no centralized routing record.
domain: Domain 2 — Implementation and Integration
task: 2.4 — Implement FM API integrations
comparison_note: Three-way group with AIPC01_D4_002 and AIPC01_D2_003 — all are 'route simple vs complex requests to different models' scenarios, but the driver behind the correct answer differs each time. Here (D2_001) the driver is operational resilience — throttling/latency fallback plus an explicit audit trail of routing decisions — which needs an orchestration layer (Step Functions) to get branching, retry, fallback, and execution history in one managed place. In D4_002 the driver is pure cost efficiency with minimal custom logic, pointing to Bedrock's own managed Intelligent Prompt Routing feature. In D2_003 the driver is also cost + avoiding GPU infra management, but the correct concept is named 'API-based model cascading' (the exam-guide term from Task 2.2) rather than the product-feature name 'Intelligent Prompt Routing' — same mechanism, different label the exam may test. Read for the requirement keyword: 'audit trail' + 'fallback on throttling' → Step Functions; 'reduce cost' + 'minimal custom logic' / 'avoid GPU management' → cascading via Intelligent Prompt Routing (Task 2.2/4.1 phrasing may vary between 'cascading' and 'Intelligent Prompt Routing').

question: A media company is building an internal GenAI assistant on Amazon Bedrock to help employees summarize meeting notes and answer policy questions. The application currently sends every user request to a high-capability (and higher-cost) model. Usage has grown, and most requests are simple summaries, while a smaller portion requires deeper reasoning and higher response quality. The team wants to reduce ongoing inference costs while preserving high-quality answers for complex requests, with minimal custom routing logic to maintain. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: A) Implement an AWS Lambda router that invokes the lower-cost model first for every request and then invokes the higher-capability model only if the first response appears incomplete. Store responses in Amazon DynamoDB for future reuse.

B) Configure Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing to route requests between a lower-cost model for simple requests and a higher-capability model for complex requests based on prompt complexity, and monitor token usage in Amazon CloudWatch.
C) Purchase provisioned throughput for the higher-capability model so the application can handle growth more efficiently and reduce cost per request.
D) Enable Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the application's system prompt and few-shot examples and continue using the same higher-capability model for all requests.
explanation: Cost-effective tiered model use with minimal custom logic points to a managed routing feature rather than a hand-built classifier/router. B) Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing natively routes simple requests to the cheaper model and complex ones to the higher-capability model based on prompt complexity, with CloudWatch token metrics for validating savings — no custom routing service to build or maintain. A) Calling the cheap model first for every request risks double invocation (cheap + expensive) on a large share of requests, and 'is the response incomplete' evaluation logic must be built and tuned — this can raise cost and latency rather than lower it. C) Provisioned throughput is a capacity/performance lever, not query-based model selection — it doesn't send simple requests to a cheaper model and can increase cost if underutilized. D) Prompt caching discounts a repeated static prefix but keeps every request on the expensive model — the core cost driver (using a high-cost model for simple work) is untouched.
domain: Domain 4 — Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
task: 4.1 — Implement cost optimization and resource efficiency strategies
comparison_note: Three-way group with AIPC01_D2_001 and AIPC01_D2_003. This question's driver is cost + minimal custom logic → Intelligent Prompt Routing (managed, purpose-built), same underlying mechanism the exam guide also calls 'API-based model cascading' in D2_003. D2_001's driver is resilience (throttling fallback) + audit trail → Step Functions orchestration instead. Don't default to one answer just because you see 'route simple vs complex' — check whether the scenario is asking about cost/GPU-avoidance (routing/cascading) or about fallback/audit requirements (Step Functions). A fourth variant, AIPC01_D2_031, routes among THREE business categories driven by content classification rather than two complexity tiers, and again uses Step Functions — but for running an explicit classification step and Choice-state branching, not a throttling fallback.

question: A global airline's disruption-management team is building a generative AI service that classifies passenger messages and generates responses by using several Amazon Bedrock foundation models. Simple itinerary questions should use a low-cost model, policy disputes should use a model tuned for reasoning, and multilingual rebooking requests should use a model with stronger language support. Existing clients send only free-form text, locale, and account tier, and the team does not want clients to choose models. The solution must keep an auditable routing path, allow routing rules to change without redeploying clients, and invoke only one generation model for each request to control cost. Which implementation will meet these requirements?
options: A) Use API Gateway to validate requests and invoke a Lambda function. Evaluate routing rules in Lambda from the message text, select a Bedrock model, and emit routing metrics to CloudWatch.
B) Use Amazon Bedrock prompt routing as the primary selector. Configure supported model choices for cost and capability tradeoffs, and send each airline message through one shared generation prompt.
C) Use API Gateway to start a Step Functions workflow. Route with Choice states based on locale and account tier, and invoke the mapped Bedrock model from a Lambda task.

D) Use API Gateway to validate requests and start a Step Functions workflow. Run a lightweight classification step, use Choice states for routing, and invoke the selected Bedrock model from a Lambda task.
explanation: Three distinct passenger-message categories driven by MESSAGE CONTENT (not just locale/tier metadata), server-side-only model selection, an auditable decision path, and exactly one generation call per request all point to explicit content classification plus Step Functions orchestration. D) A lightweight classification step examines the actual message content to determine category; Choice states route to the mapped model; only one Lambda task (and therefore one model) is invoked per request; Step Functions execution history gives the audit trail, and routing rules live in the workflow/classifier, not client code — changeable without redeploying clients. A) A Lambda-only rules engine can keep selection server-side and invoke one model, but it gives much less explicit, inspectable workflow-level auditability than Step Functions execution history as routing paths grow. B) Bedrock prompt routing optimizes model selection for supported routing behavior, but it doesn't give the application-controlled semantic classification and branch-level audit trail needed to distinguish airline-specific business categories like policy disputes vs. itinerary questions. C) Routing only on locale and account tier can't reliably distinguish an itinerary question from a policy dispute or rebooking request that share the same locale/tier — it misses the actual content-based classification requirement.
domain: Domain 2 — Implementation and Integration
task: 2.1 — Implement agentic AI solutions and tool integrations
comparison_note: A fourth variant in the model-routing family alongside AIPC01_D2_001, AIPC01_D4_002, and AIPC01_D2_003 (see AIPC01_D4_002's note for the full three-way breakdown). Those three route between exactly two tiers (simple vs. complex) driven by throttling-fallback/audit (Step Functions), cost/minimal-logic (Intelligent Prompt Routing), or cost/GPU-avoidance (cascading). This question routes among THREE distinct business categories driven by semantic CONTENT classification, and again lands on Step Functions — but here the Step Functions role is running an explicit classification step plus Choice-state branching to enforce single-model invocation and audit visibility, not implementing a throttling fallback. If the routing driver is 'classify free-form content into business categories, keep it auditable, invoke only one model' → Step Functions with a classification step (this pattern).

question: A retail platform is building a GenAI feature that helps sellers create product listing text by using Amazon Bedrock. Most requests are routine (for example, short rewrites and basic summaries), but a smaller percentage require more advanced reasoning and higher-quality copy. The team wants to reduce ongoing inference costs while still producing high-quality output for complex requests, and the solution must avoid managing GPU infrastructure. Which deployment approach is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
options: A) Use a single large text model in Amazon Bedrock for all requests. Purchase provisioned throughput to ensure consistent performance during peak traffic.

B) Implement API-based model cascading in Amazon Bedrock: route routine listing requests to a smaller pre-trained model and automatically escalate complex requests to a larger model (for example, by using intelligent prompt routing or application-side routing logic).
C) Fine-tune a large Amazon Bedrock custom model so it can handle both routine and complex listing requests with shorter prompts, then use that single custom model for all invocations.
D) Deploy an open-source LLM on a GPU-backed Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint and use the endpoint for all listing-generation requests to control performance.
explanation: Matching model capability to request complexity — cheap model for the routine majority, larger model only for the complex minority — is the exam-guide concept of 'API-based model cascading' (Task 2.2), and it stays fully within managed Bedrock so no GPU infrastructure needs to be operated. B) is exactly this: small pre-trained model handles routine rewrites/summaries, escalation (via intelligent routing or app-side logic) reserves the larger model for complex requests. A) A single large model for everything keeps cost high on the routine majority regardless of provisioned throughput — throughput solves consistency, not cost-to-complexity matching. C) Fine-tuning one large custom model for both cases is expensive and still applies the same heavyweight model to every request — no cascading, no cost reduction for the routine majority. D) A GPU-backed SageMaker real-time endpoint directly violates the 'avoid managing GPU infrastructure' requirement and applies the same heavyweight deployment to every request regardless of complexity.
domain: Domain 2 — Implementation and Integration
task: 2.2 — Implement model deployment strategies
comparison_note: Three-way group with AIPC01_D2_001 and AIPC01_D4_002 — see AIPC01_D4_002's note for the full breakdown. Key giveaway here: 'avoid managing GPU infrastructure' + 'reduce ongoing inference costs' + routine-vs-complex split → cascading/routing (this question and D4_002 share the same underlying answer, just named 'API-based model cascading' vs 'Intelligent Prompt Routing' — both point to tiered model selection, not to Step Functions orchestration, which is reserved for the resilience/audit-trail variant in D2_001).

question: An insurance company is building a GenAI workflow that processes claims descriptions in multiple languages and varying complexity and uses different specialized models for triage, summarization, and risk classification. The company wants to select the appropriate model based on language, token length, and content category and also evolve routing rules over time using performance metrics such as latency, cost, and human quality scores stored in an operational metrics store. You are responsible for designing an orchestration workflow that can apply content based routing, use metric driven rules for model selection, and support confidence based cascading between models. Which two approaches should you implement to design this intelligent routing workflow so that it can adapt to content characteristics and observed model performance? (Select two)
options: A) Implement a single Lambda function with hardcoded if else rules to select models based on language and token length and store metrics only as CloudWatch Logs. Rely on manual review of CloudWatch dashboards to determine when to update or redeploy routing rules.

B) Use Step Functions Choice states with routing rules fixed by values stored in Parameter Store and update thresholds manually through configuration changes. Write latency and quality metrics to DynamoDB but use them only for offline dashboards rather than feeding them into the real time routing logic.

C) Use Step Functions with a Lambda pre processing task to compute language, token length, and content attributes and pass them to Choice states for routing to the triage, summarization, or risk classification model. Store performance metrics in DynamoDB and have a Lambda task read these metrics at runtime to adjust routing thresholds dynamically.

D) Use Step Functions Map or Parallel states to branch decisions and insert a metrics evaluation Lambda task that reads historical performance data to compute confidence scores before selecting the model. Implement a cascading workflow that invokes a primary model first and conditionally calls a backup model when confidence or quality thresholds from the metrics store are not met.

E) Use Step Functions with a Lambda pre processing task that computes language and token length, then call a metrics evaluation Lambda function to read latency and quality data from DynamoDB before routing to a Bedrock model. Apply Choice states only after the model inference step so the workflow can examine the generated output and decide whether to invoke a backup model.
explanation: Two complementary mechanisms make this adaptive: content-attribute routing decided BEFORE invocation, and a metrics-driven confidence check that can trigger a backup call AFTER a primary model runs. C) Pre-processing computes language/token-length/content-category attributes and feeds Choice states to route proactively to the right specialized model; storing metrics in DynamoDB and reading them at runtime lets routing thresholds adapt to real latency/cost/quality trends without redeployment. D) Map/Parallel states plus a metrics-evaluation Lambda compute confidence scores from historical performance data, enabling a genuine CASCADE: invoke the primary model, and only call a backup when confidence/quality thresholds (drawn from the live metrics store) aren't met — a post-hoc safety net layered on top of the proactive routing in C. A) Hardcoded if/else Lambda rules require code redeployment for any threshold change, and metrics-only-in-CloudWatch-Logs with manual dashboard review provides no automated, real-time adaptation at all. B) Static Parameter Store thresholds updated manually, with metrics written to DynamoDB but never consulted by the routing logic, means the system behaves identically regardless of actual model performance — metric-driven adaptation and confidence cascading are both absent. E) Applying Choice states only AFTER model inference forces every request through at least one model call regardless of content type, wasting capacity and increasing latency — routing must happen proactively based on content BEFORE the first invocation, not only reactively after.
domain: Domain 2 — Implementation and Integration
task: 2.1 — Implement agentic AI solutions and tool integrations
comparison_note: Distinguishes two different meanings of 'cascading' that can otherwise blur together. AIPC01_D2_003's 'API-based model cascading' is COMPLEXITY-based and decided BEFORE any invocation: classify the request as routine or complex, then send it to the appropriate tier — the smaller model is never invoked for complex requests at all. This question's cascading (option D) is CONFIDENCE-based and decided AFTER the primary model has already run: invoke the primary model, evaluate its output confidence/quality against live metrics-store thresholds, and only THEN conditionally call a backup — a post-hoc safety net, not a pre-invocation tier selection. Both are valid 'cascading' patterns under the exam's terminology, but they trigger at opposite points in the request lifecycle — read the scenario for whether the decision happens before invocation (complexity-based) or after seeing a result (confidence-based).

question: A multimodal image and text analysis pipeline currently calls a single, large foundation model for every request, regardless of whether the user needs a simple label or a detailed explanation, which increases cost and creates bottlenecks during peak load. Internal analysis shows that many requests could be handled by a smaller, cheaper model without affecting accuracy, while only a subset truly requires the advanced reasoning capabilities of the larger model. The platform team suspects they could reduce costs by splitting the workflow into cheaper classification steps and only invoking the more capable model when necessary. As a GenAI engineer, how should you implement a solution to optimize cost while preserving output quality for complex workloads?
options: A) Migrate the large multimodal model to a larger instance type on SageMaker and enable Provisioned Throughput on Amazon Bedrock so that all requests continue to call the same model with lower latency. Rely on the increased capacity to absorb traffic without introducing additional routing or staged inference logic.

B) Precompute simple labels for all images offline using a SageMaker training job and store them in Amazon DynamoDB, but still invoke the large multimodal model online for every incoming request to maintain a consistent experience. Use the stored labels only as metadata in responses rather than as a decision point for bypassing the multimodal model.

C) Set up an Amazon SageMaker inference pipeline where a lightweight classifier runs first and forwards its prediction to the multimodal model so that both models contribute to the final answer. Always invoke the multimodal model to confirm or refine the classifier output to maintain consistent response quality.

D) Configure an Amazon SageMaker inference pipeline where a first, cheaper model hosted on SageMaker performs image or text classification and confidence scoring, and only call an Amazon Bedrock multimodal model in a later stage when the request requires detailed reasoning or the classifier has low confidence. Use routing logic in the pipeline container to short circuit the workflow and return early for simple label requests so that the multimodal model is invoked only when needed.
explanation: Real cost savings from a cascade require the cheap model to genuinely GATE access to the expensive one — some requests must never reach the expensive model at all. D) A SageMaker inference pipeline chains a cheap classifier (with confidence scoring) before the Bedrock multimodal model; routing logic SHORT-CIRCUITS the workflow, returning the classifier result directly for simple/high-confidence cases and only escalating to the expensive model when reasoning is needed or confidence is low — a genuine subset of traffic never reaches the costly model. A) Upsizing the single model plus provisioned throughput improves latency/capacity but every request STILL calls the most expensive model — no differentiation between simple and complex tasks, so the core cost problem remains untouched. B) Precomputed offline labels are stored but never used as a ROUTING decision — the multimodal model is still invoked for every request regardless, eliminating any cost benefit from having the labels at all. C) The classifier runs first, but the multimodal model is ALWAYS invoked afterward to 'confirm or refine' — this is a serial enrichment pipeline, not a true gate, and produces nearly the same compute cost and latency as the original single-model architecture since the expensive model still runs every time.
domain: Domain 2 — Implementation and Integration
task: 2.2 — Implement model deployment strategies
comparison_note: The concrete SageMaker-native implementation of the general cascading concept in AIPC01_D2_003 ('API-based model cascading') — same principle (cheap tier handles the routine majority, expensive tier reserved for the minority that needs it), here expressed specifically as chained containers on one SageMaker inference pipeline with confidence-based short-circuit logic. Distinct from AIPC01_D2_036's confidence-based cascading: there, a FULL PRIMARY GENERATION model runs first and its OUTPUT is quality-checked before conditionally calling a backup. Here, a lightweight CLASSIFIER (not a full generation call) runs first, and ITS confidence score decides whether to short-circuit (return the classifier result) or escalate to the expensive model — the cheap first stage is classification, not a complete generation attempt.

question: A healthcare platform team is enabling multiple product groups to build GenAI applications on AWS by using Amazon Bedrock. The applications will be deployed in different AWS accounts and environments (dev, test, and production). The platform team must provide a consistent, repeatable way for teams to implement GenAI architectures that align with organizational best practices across security, reliability, and cost. Which approach will achieve this with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: A) Create a custom internal architecture review system by using AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon API Gateway to enforce a proprietary checklist for every GenAI deployment.

B) Use the AWS Well-Architected Tool with the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens to define and review a standard GenAI architecture. Provide approved reusable infrastructure-as-code components (for example, AWS CDK or AWS CloudFormation templates) that teams can deploy across accounts and environments.

C) Grant each product group permissions to use the Amazon Bedrock console playground to prototype their solution, and use AWS CloudTrail logs after deployment to verify that teams followed organizational standards.
D) Use AWS Organizations service control policies (SCPs) to restrict which AWS Regions and services can be used, and require all teams to use the same foundation model for every GenAI workload.
explanation: Low-overhead, repeatable standardization across many teams/accounts needs an established best-practices framework plus reusable technical building blocks — not a custom-built tool or purely reactive/restrictive control. B) The Well-Architected Tool + Generative AI Lens gives a managed, pillar-aligned review mechanism, and approved CDK/CloudFormation components let teams deploy the same vetted architecture repeatedly with minimal ongoing effort. A) Building a proprietary Lambda/DynamoDB/API Gateway review system duplicates what Well-Architected already provides and adds a system the platform team must build and maintain. C) Playground prototyping plus after-the-fact CloudTrail auditing is reactive — it catches deviations after deployment rather than standardizing design/implementation up front. D) SCPs are governance guardrails (Region/service restrictions) and forcing a single FM doesn't standardize architecture — it doesn't address the security/reliability/cost best-practices consistency the team actually needs.
domain: Domain 1 — Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
task: 1.1 — Analyze requirements and design GenAI solutions
comparison_note: Near-duplicate of AIPC01_D1_025 — same winning pattern (Well-Architected Tool + Generative AI Lens, paired with approved reusable IaC components) reused with a different industry framing (healthcare vs. electric utility). D1_025 sharpens the point further by explicitly contrasting the GenAI Lens against 'only the standard [Well-Architected] pillars' as a distractor — reinforcing that generic Well-Architected review misses GenAI-specific concerns (guardrails, retrieval patterns, responsible AI) that only the Generative AI Lens covers.

question: An electric utility's grid operations software team is enabling several product teams to build Amazon Bedrock applications, including outage summarization, maintenance procedure Q&A, and regulatory report drafting. The product teams deploy independently in separate AWS accounts and sometimes use different RAG data sources, but the security office has found inconsistent IAM boundaries, guardrail use, logging, and retrieval patterns. The platform team must provide a reusable standard that teams can adopt without waiting for manual design approval, and must produce repeatable architecture review evidence for each deployment. Which approach will meet these requirements MOST effectively?
options: A) Publish reusable AWS CDK constructs for approved Bedrock integration patterns, and assess each deployment in AWS Well-Architected Tool by applying only the standard pillars.
B) Publish a shared Bedrock proxy service for approved Bedrock integration patterns, and assess each deployment by reviewing proxy invocation logs centrally.
C) Publish reusable CloudFormation stacks for approved Bedrock integration patterns, and assess each deployment by storing checklist results in a shared repository.
D) Publish reusable AWS CDK constructs for approved Bedrock integration patterns, and assess each deployment in AWS Well-Architected Tool by applying the Generative AI Lens.
explanation: Independent teams across separate accounts need self-serve reusable building blocks (no manual approval bottleneck) plus a GenAI-specific structured review mechanism that produces repeatable evidence. D) Reusable CDK constructs encode approved defaults (IAM boundaries, guardrail use, logging, retrieval wiring) that teams adopt directly, no waiting for manual design approval; the Well-Architected Tool with the Generative AI Lens specifically covers GenAI-relevant review areas (model selection, data integration, responsible AI, deployment) and produces a structured, repeatable risk/improvement-plan record per workload. A) Standard pillars alone miss the GenAI-specific guidance (guardrails, retrieval patterns, responsible AI) that's exactly the inconsistency the security office found — the Generative AI Lens is what closes that gap. B) A shared proxy centralizes some controls but becomes a coupling point that conflicts with teams needing different RAG sources and independent deployment patterns, and proxy logs aren't the same as structured architecture review evidence. C) Reusable CloudFormation can standardize infrastructure, but static checklist files stored in a repository don't provide the same structured review, risk-tracking, and improvement-planning workflow — more prone to drift and inconsistent evidence.
domain: Domain 1 — Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
task: 1.1 — Analyze requirements and design GenAI solutions
comparison_note: Near-duplicate of AIPC01_D1_004 — same winning pattern (AWS Well-Architected Tool + the Generative AI Lens, paired with approved reusable infrastructure-as-code components) reused with a different industry (electric utility vs. healthcare) and slightly different IaC choice (CDK constructs here vs. CDK/CloudFormation templates there). The added nuance in this version: it explicitly contrasts the GenAI Lens against using 'only the standard pillars' as a distractor, sharpening the point that generic Well-Architected review misses GenAI-specific concerns (guardrails, retrieval patterns, responsible AI) that a plain infrastructure standard or checklist wouldn't catch either.

question: A fintech company is launching a public, GenAI-powered customer support chatbot that uses Amazon Bedrock to answer account questions. Security reviewers are concerned about prompt injection attempts (for example, users trying to override instructions or request hidden system prompts) and about accidental leakage of personally identifiable information (PII) in both user inputs and model outputs. The company wants a defense-in-depth approach that adds comprehensive protection against FM misuse with the LEAST operational overhead. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: A) Implement a serverless safety pipeline where Amazon API Gateway invokes a Lambda function that uses Amazon Comprehend to detect and mask PII in user prompts before invoking Amazon Bedrock with Bedrock Guardrails enabled. After the model responds, the Lambda function performs post-processing validation and additional PII redaction before returning the response through API Gateway response mapping templates that enforce a safe, filtered response shape.

B) Place Amazon API Gateway in front of the chatbot. Use AWS WAF managed rules to block SQL injection and common web exploits, and then invoke Amazon Bedrock directly from the application with no additional controls.

C) Fine-tune a custom model in Amazon Bedrock by using past chat transcripts so the model learns the company's policies and avoids unsafe outputs. Deploy the fine-tuned model without additional pre-processing or post-processing because the model has been customized.

D) Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails only, configured to block profanity and remove PII. Rely on the guardrail blocked-message response to prevent misuse, and return the model response directly to callers.
explanation: Defense-in-depth means layering independent controls so a single miss (bad detection, injection variant, integration bug) doesn't expose PII or allow misuse. A) stacks Comprehend pre-processing PII masking, Bedrock Guardrails model-native filtering, Lambda post-processing redaction, and API Gateway response shaping into a filtered contract — all managed/serverless, so low ops overhead with real layering. B) WAF protects the HTTP layer against web exploits (SQLi etc.) but has no concept of PII, prompt injection, or output moderation — it's the wrong layer entirely, and there's no LLM-specific control at all. C) Fine-tuning on transcripts might shift model behavior stylistically but doesn't guarantee safety compliance and is not a substitute for runtime layered controls — it's also costlier than guardrails/pre-post processing. D) Guardrails alone is only a single layer; it's a necessary piece but not sufficient for defense-in-depth since it has no independent backstop for missed detections or novel injection patterns.
domain: Domain 3 — AI Safety, Security, and Governance
task: 3.1 — Implement input and output safety controls
comparison_note: Contrast with AIPC01_D3_009 — the SAME 'Guardrails only' option that is WRONG here (this question explicitly asks for 'defense-in-depth' / 'comprehensive protection', so a single layer isn't enough) is the CORRECT answer in D3_009, which only asks for real-time protection with least operational overhead and never asks for defense-in-depth. Read the requirement wording: 'defense-in-depth' / 'comprehensive' → build the full layered stack (this question's answer); plain 'real-time' + 'least overhead' with no defense-in-depth language → Guardrails alone is correct (D3_009's answer).

question: A healthcare technology team is building a patient-facing virtual assistant that uses a text foundation model (FM) on Amazon Bedrock to answer questions about appointment scheduling. The assistant is exposed through a public API and has recently received user messages containing profanity, harassment, and attempts to override the assistant's instructions (prompt injection). The team also must ensure that personally identifiable information (PII) such as phone numbers and social security numbers in user messages is masked before the FM processes the request. Which solution will protect against harmful user inputs in real time with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: A) Create an AWS Step Functions workflow that sends each prompt to a human review queue for approval before invoking the Amazon Bedrock model. Reject prompts that contain harmful content or prompt injection attempts.

B) Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail that uses topic and word filtering (including profanity) and input PII masking. Configure the application's Bedrock model invocation to apply the guardrail and return a standard blocked message when the guardrail intervenes.
C) Store each user message in Amazon S3 and run an Amazon Macie discovery job to detect PII. After the discovery job completes, invoke the FM on Amazon Bedrock by using the sanitized text.

D) Use AWS WAF in front of Amazon API Gateway to block requests that contain profanity and common prompt-injection strings. Pass all remaining requests directly to Amazon Bedrock without additional safety controls.
explanation: The requirement here is real-time input protection with the LEAST operational overhead — no explicit call for a multi-layer defense-in-depth stack — so a single well-configured managed control is the right-sized answer. B) A Bedrock guardrail with topic/word filtering (profanity, harassment categories) plus input PII masking runs as part of the model invocation itself: one managed, real-time control covering both the harmful-input and PII requirements with minimal custom code. A) Human review adds latency incompatible with real-time conversational use and is excessive operational overhead for baseline, high-volume filtering. C) Macie is a scheduled/batch S3 discovery tool, not a real-time request-path control — wrong latency profile entirely. D) WAF can block some known string patterns at the web layer but isn't a GenAI-aware safety system — it has no PII masking capability and can't reliably catch subtle prompt injection or nuanced harmful content the way a model-aware guardrail can.
domain: Domain 3 — AI Safety, Security, and Governance
task: 3.1 — Implement input and output safety controls
comparison_note: Compare with AIPC01_D3_001 — the SAME 'Guardrails only' option is CORRECT here but WRONG there, which makes this the highest-value contrast pair in the safety-controls task. D3_001 explicitly asks for a 'defense-in-depth approach' with 'comprehensive protection' — under that explicit framing, Guardrails-alone is deliberately insufficient (no independent backstop for missed detections), and the correct answer layers Comprehend pre-processing + Guardrails + Lambda post-processing + API Gateway response shaping. This question (D3_009) asks only for real-time protection with the LEAST operational overhead — no 'defense-in-depth' or 'comprehensive' language — so the single-layer Guardrails control (topic/word filtering + PII masking) is the right-sized, correct answer; adding extra layers here would be over-engineering relative to what was asked. Read the requirement wording carefully: 'defense-in-depth' / 'comprehensive protection' → build the full layered stack; plain 'real-time protection' + 'least operational overhead' with no defense-in-depth language → Guardrails alone is sufficient and correct. A third example of this same pattern is AIPC01_D3_013 — another 'Guardrails only, simplest approach, least overhead' scenario with no defense-in-depth language, where Guardrails alone is again correct.

question: A fintech development team is building a customer-facing chat assistant that invokes an Amazon Bedrock text model through an AWS Lambda function. The assistant must block harmful user inputs (such as profanity and requests about disallowed topics) before they influence model behavior, and the team wants the simplest approach that can be applied consistently across the application. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: A) Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with topic filtering and word filtering. Attach the guardrail to the model invocation so that blocked inputs return a standard blocked message.
B) Store approved prompts in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management and require a manual approval workflow for all prompts before the application can send them to the model.
C) Use an Amazon API Gateway request validator with a JSON Schema model to enforce a strict request format. Add a system prompt telling the model to refuse any request that contains unsafe content.
D) Configure AWS WAF on Amazon API Gateway with regex pattern matching to detect harmful prompts and block requests that match those patterns before invoking the Lambda function.
explanation: The requirement is explicitly 'the simplest approach applied consistently' with least operational overhead — no defense-in-depth or comprehensive-protection language — so a single managed control is right-sized. A) A Bedrock guardrail with topic and word filtering, attached directly to the model invocation, centralizes content safety in one managed place and returns a consistent blocked message across the whole application — exactly the simplest consistent control. B) Prompt Management governs developer-authored reusable templates, not real-time end-user input moderation, and a manual approval workflow is impractical (and high-overhead) for interactive chat. C) Schema validation only checks request structure, not content safety, and a system-prompt-only 'please refuse unsafe content' instruction is vulnerable to prompt injection — not a robust control. D) WAF regex matching is a web-layer pattern tool, not a GenAI-aware safety system — it can't reliably classify nuanced disallowed topics or harmful natural language the way a guardrail can.
domain: Domain 3 — AI Safety, Security, and Governance
task: 3.1 — Implement input and output safety controls
comparison_note: Third entry in the 'Guardrails only' pattern group alongside AIPC01_D3_001 and AIPC01_D3_009 (see D3_009's note for the full breakdown). Reinforces the same rule: when a question asks only for simple/consistent/least-overhead input protection (as here — no 'defense-in-depth' or 'comprehensive protection' wording), Guardrails alone is correct. Only when the scenario explicitly demands a defense-in-depth or comprehensive stack (as in D3_001) does Guardrails-alone become insufficient.

question: A global video game studio's trust and safety team is building a real-time NPC chat feature by using Amazon Bedrock. The feature must block harmful player prompts before they reach the foundation model, mask sensitive information in model responses, enforce studio-specific banned topics, and send only ambiguous moderation cases to a human review process. Normal conversations must stay on the synchronous request path with minimal added latency. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: A) Run each chat turn through a Step Functions Express workflow, invoke Lambda pre-checks, apply a Bedrock guardrail during inference, and branch to human review for ambiguous cases.
B) Run a custom Lambda moderation service before Bedrock, use Amazon Comprehend for entity detection, mask responses in Lambda, and start Step Functions only for low-confidence cases.
C) Apply an Amazon Bedrock guardrail only to model responses in the gateway Lambda, add Lambda checks for player prompts, and start Step Functions only for human review exceptions.
D) Apply an Amazon Bedrock guardrail to prompts and responses in the gateway Lambda, add Lambda checks for studio-specific policies, and start Step Functions only for human review exceptions.
explanation: Real-time synchronous chat with minimal latency needs the broad safety coverage handled inline by a managed guardrail, narrow custom logic kept lightweight, and orchestration reserved ONLY for the actual exception path — not injected into every normal turn. D) A Bedrock guardrail applied to BOTH prompts and responses in the gateway Lambda covers harmful-content blocking (input) and PII masking (output) inline on the synchronous path; Lambda adds narrow studio-specific checks guardrails don't cover; Step Functions only starts for human-review exceptions, keeping normal conversations fast and simple. A) Routing every normal chat turn through a Step Functions Express workflow adds orchestration overhead and latency to the common case — even though guardrails are still used, this doesn't minimize overhead for the vast majority of normal turns. B) Custom Lambda+Comprehend moderation shifts broad harmful-content filtering and topic/output-safety handling into hand-built logic instead of using managed guardrails inline — more development and tuning overhead. C) Guardrail applied only to RESPONSES, not prompts — harmful player prompts would reach the FM unfiltered, failing the 'block before reaching the model' requirement; custom Lambda checks become the primary INPUT safety control, which is weaker coverage than a managed guardrail.
domain: Domain 3 — AI Safety, Security, and Governance
task: 3.1 — Implement input and output safety controls
comparison_note: Reinforces the 'Guardrails alone (on both prompts and responses) is often sufficient for the main path' family (AIPC01_D3_001/D3_009/D3_013), and adds a new architectural pattern those questions didn't need: reserve Step Functions orchestration strictly for the EXCEPTION path (ambiguous cases needing human review), never for the normal synchronous request — orchestrating every turn (as in this question's wrong answer A) adds latency and overhead the low-latency requirement rules out.

question: A digital assistant answers user questions across multiple business functions, including customer support, product usage, and general knowledge. During internal reviews, teams observe that some user inputs contain aggressive or explicit phrasing that varies in severity, while other inputs request guidance in domains, such as investment advice, that the company has decided the assistant should never address, even when the request is phrased in a neutral or professional manner. The platform team wants to enforce consistent safeguards at inference time.
