A) Historical query-similarity matching bypasses actual document-based grounding entirely — it can't reflect fresh seasonal data or current hotel availability, and provides no decomposition, expansion, or targeted retrieval at all. B) Rewriting the WHOLE query with one Bedrock call still produces a single monolithic query passed through one retrieval call — without decomposition, a single embedding vector still compresses multiple distinct intents (dates, amenities, location) together, losing constraint-specific precision. C) Generating a preliminary itinerary with the FM FIRST, then extracting keywords from that ungrounded output for a second retrieval, creates a circular dependency where retrieval quality depends on an already-ungrounded generation — this loses semantic nuance (seasonal constraints, family suitability) and undermines the grounding the pipeline is meant to provide.
domain: Domain 1 — Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
task: 1.5 — Design retrieval mechanisms for FM augmentation
comparison_note: Near-duplicate of AIPC01_D1_020 — same core architecture (Step Functions orchestrating a Lambda-driven query decomposition into intent-specific subqueries, each retrieved separately, then merged/aggregated before final generation). This question adds an explicit QUERY EXPANSION step (a Bedrock model enriches each subquery with standardized phrasing and explicit constraints before searching) that D1_020 didn't call out as a distinct stage — otherwise, both reinforce the same lesson: decompose a multi-intent question into separately-retrieved subqueries rather than sending one raw or lightly-rewritten query through a single retrieval call.

question: A global architectural design firm's knowledge management team is launching a generative AI assistant for employees. The assistant must answer questions from SharePoint, Amazon S3 project archives, and Jira, and must take actions in approved business systems. The firm uses an enterprise identity provider that is already connected to AWS IAM Identity Center. The security team requires per-user authorization to be enforced from the source systems where possible, centralized user and group assignment, and minimal custom code for access-control decisions. Which implementation will BEST meet these requirements?
options: A) Deploy an Amazon Kendra index, federate users through a SAML identity provider, connect the index to a Bedrock agent, and implement actions through Lambda.
B) Deploy an Amazon Q Business application, connect it to IAM Identity Center, configure supported data connectors and plugins, and assign access by users and groups.
C) Deploy an API Gateway front end, authorize requests with IAM roles, invoke Amazon Bedrock directly from Lambda, and restrict source access with bucket policies.
D) Deploy an Amazon Bedrock agent, federate users through Amazon Cognito, store document ACLs as vector metadata, and apply retrieval filters in each request.
explanation: A managed, multi-source, action-taking enterprise assistant with source-system-enforced per-user authorization and centralized group assignment is exactly Amazon Q Business's designed scope. B) Q Business connects to IAM Identity Center for centralized workforce identity/group assignment, and its supported connectors/plugins for SharePoint, S3, and Jira preserve source-system authorization context so responses are limited to what the signed-in user can access — minimal custom access-control code. A) Kendra can do enterprise search with user-context filtering, but building a full action-taking assistant on top of it still requires substantial custom integration — more custom code than the requirement wants. C) IAM roles + bucket policies authorize API/S3 access, not document-level permissions from SharePoint/Jira — this leaves per-user source authorization essentially unenforced, requiring significant custom logic to fix. D) Storing ACLs as vector metadata and applying retrieval filters per request is a fully custom authorization system — real ongoing engineering to keep ACLs and group membership synchronized across sources, the opposite of minimal custom code.
domain: Domain 2 — Implementation and Integration
task: 2.3 — Design and implement enterprise integration architectures
comparison_note: Loosely related to AIPC01_D2_012 — both involve IAM Identity Center federation, but for different consumers. D2_012 federates individual DEVELOPERS for direct programmatic Bedrock Runtime inference access (least-privilege API calls from scripts). This question federates END USERS (employees) into a managed multi-source assistant application (Amazon Q Business) where per-document authorization is enforced by the connectors themselves, not by an IAM policy scoping API actions. Same identity-federation building block, different application layer and authorization mechanism. Also see AIPC01_D2_024 for the Q-family contrast: this question uses Q Business for enterprise employee document Q&A/actions; D2_024 uses Q Developer for IDE-embedded developer tooling (chat, inline suggestions, refactoring, security scans) — same product family, different target audience.

question: A digital textbook platform's engineering productivity team is standardizing how developers build generative AI features that use AWS Lambda, AWS CDK, and Amazon Bedrock APIs. Developers work in Visual Studio Code and JetBrains IDEs. The team needs help with AWS SDK questions, code suggestions and refactoring in the IDE, repository coding guidance, and security issue identification before pull requests. The team wants the fastest path with the least custom integration. Which approach will meet these requirements MOST effectively?
options: A) Create Amazon Q Apps for the engineering organization. Build reusable workflow apps for code review checklists, prompt templates, and issue tracking updates through approved plugins.
B) Deploy Amazon Q Business for the engineering organization. Connect source repositories and AWS documentation, and expose custom plugins for pull request and build workflow actions.
C) Create an Amazon Bedrock agent for the engineering organization. Index AWS documentation in a knowledge base, and use action groups to run lint, test, and build commands.
D) Deploy Amazon Q Developer in the approved IDEs. Configure project guidance, and use chat, inline suggestions, refactoring support, and security scans during pull request preparation.
explanation: IDE-native chat, inline code suggestions, refactoring, and pre-PR security scanning is exactly the software-development-lifecycle scope Amazon Q Developer targets natively. D) Q Developer integrates directly into VS Code and JetBrains, giving AWS SDK guidance, inline suggestions, code transformation/refactoring, and security scans as a built-in experience — fastest path, no custom integration to build. A) Q Apps builds no-code workflow apps for business processes (checklists, templates) — not IDE-native code generation or security scanning. B) Q Business is an enterprise employee assistant over connected knowledge/apps — even with repo connectors and custom plugins, it doesn't provide the IDE-embedded coding experience developers need, and building that would require real custom work. C) A custom Bedrock agent with a KB and action groups could technically approximate parts of this, but it requires building and maintaining the entire integration and workflow — the opposite of 'least custom integration.'
domain: Domain 2 — Implementation and Integration
task: 2.5 — Implement application integration patterns and development tools
comparison_note: Compare with AIPC01_D2_019 for a useful Q-family distinction: that question uses Amazon Q Business for an ENTERPRISE EMPLOYEE assistant answering questions across SharePoint/S3/Jira with per-user document authorization. This question uses Amazon Q Developer for IDE-EMBEDDED DEVELOPER tooling (chat, inline suggestions, refactoring, security scans). Same 'Q' product family, different target audience and integration surface: business knowledge workers connecting to enterprise data sources → Q Business; developers working inside VS Code/JetBrains → Q Developer. Picking the wrong one means either exposing employees to a code-editor-only tool or trying to force Q Developer to do enterprise document Q&A it isn't built for.

question: A museum consortium's visitor-experience engineering team is adding a GenAI question-answering feature to an existing web application. The frontend will call an HTTPS microservice and can wait for a complete response. The team wants the least complex serverless integration that preserves a common conversation request pattern when switching among Amazon Bedrock text models that support messages. The API and integration will be deployed with AWS CloudFormation. Which implementation best meets these requirements?
options: A) Create an API Gateway REST API with a Lambda proxy integration and a stage deployment. Grant API Gateway permission to invoke the function, and have Lambda call Converse on bedrock-runtime with bedrock:InvokeModel permission.

B) Create an API Gateway HTTP API with a Lambda proxy integration that specifies payloadFormatVersion 2.0. Grant API Gateway permission to invoke the function, and have Lambda call InvokeModel with one shared JSON body for all selected models.

C) Create an API Gateway HTTP API with a Lambda proxy integration that specifies payloadFormatVersion 2.0. Grant API Gateway permission to invoke the function, and have Lambda call Converse on the Amazon Bedrock service endpoint with streaming permission.

D) Create an API Gateway HTTP API with a Lambda proxy integration that specifies payloadFormatVersion 2.0. Grant API Gateway permission to invoke the function, and have Lambda call Converse on bedrock-runtime with bedrock:InvokeModel permission.
explanation: Two design choices matter here: the lightest-weight API layer for a synchronous HTTPS microservice, and the most portable Bedrock inference API across models. D) An HTTP API (the documented lower-latency, lighter-weight option vs REST API) with a Lambda proxy integration specifying payloadFormatVersion 2.0 gives the least complex serverless front door; calling Converse on bedrock-runtime with bedrock:InvokeModel gives a consistent message-style request interface that works across supported models without per-model request-shape branching. A) A REST API with Lambda proxy technically works and calls Converse correctly, but AWS positions REST APIs as the more feature-rich/customizable option and HTTP APIs as the lighter-weight fit for exactly this kind of lightweight integration. B) InvokeModel's body uses model-specific inference parameters — assuming one shared JSON body works across all selected models breaks the 'common conversation pattern when switching models' requirement. C) Converse is only available on the bedrock-runtime endpoint, not the general bedrock service endpoint, and a complete non-streaming Converse call requires bedrock:InvokeModel, not a streaming-specific permission.
domain: Domain 2 — Implementation and Integration
task: 2.4 — Implement FM API integrations

question: A national insurance carrier's claims integration team is modernizing an existing service bus that already exposes HTTPS APIs to internal claims systems. The team is adding Amazon Bedrock capabilities through a small adapter service. One integration path will support a claims-assistant chat experience and should make it easy to switch among Bedrock models that support message-style conversations. Another integration path will call specialized Bedrock models for image generation and embedding generation, and those calls must preserve model-specific request parameters. The adapter must avoid routing failures caused by using the wrong Bedrock endpoint or payload contract. Which TWO implementation actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)
options: A) Route all adapter traffic to the regional bedrock-runtime endpoint by using Chat Completions as the single payload contract.
B) Route image and embedding requests through the Converse API so the adapter can use one message schema for every model.
C) Route specialized generation requests to InvokeModel with application/json request bodies that match each selected model schema.
D) Route message-style assistant requests to the regional bedrock-runtime endpoint by using the Converse API for supported chat models.
E) Route every request through InvokeModel with a generic cross-model JSON body and omit contentType when accept is JSON.
explanation: Two workload types need two different Bedrock inference APIs matched to their contract needs — a consistent message interface for portable chat, and direct model-specific payloads for specialized generation. D) Converse on bedrock-runtime is the documented consistent interface for models that support messages — exactly right for a chat experience meant to be portable across supported models. C) InvokeModel with application/json bodies matching each selected model's specific schema is the right fit for image/embedding models, which need model-specific parameters that a unified chat interface can't represent. A) 'Chat Completions' isn't a real Bedrock payload contract, and no single contract works for every inference pattern regardless of endpoint correctness. B) Converse is a consistent interface for MESSAGE-capable models, not a universal schema for image or embedding generation — those need InvokeModel's model-specific bodies. E) A generic cross-model JSON body doesn't satisfy per-model InvokeModel schemas, and contentType must explicitly be application/json for InvokeModel — it can't be omitted.
domain: Domain 2 — Implementation and Integration
task: 2.4 — Implement FM API integrations
comparison_note: Reinforces the same Converse-vs-InvokeModel principle as AIPC01_D2_020, extended to a mixed-modality adapter. D2_020 is a simpler single-path decision: pick Converse (not InvokeModel) for a portable multi-model CHAT microservice. This question shows both APIs used correctly side-by-side in one adapter: Converse for the message-style chat path, InvokeModel for the specialized image/embedding paths — the underlying rule is identical (Converse = consistent message interface; InvokeModel = model-specific direct access), just applied to two different traffic types within the same system.

question: An online legal research platform's AI operations team runs a RAG assistant by using Amazon Bedrock managed knowledge bases backed by Amazon OpenSearch Serverless. The team must detect retrieval throttling and failures, identify OpenSearch Serverless indexing and search issues, and trace ingestion failures back to individual source documents while inspecting chunk creation, deletion, and failure statistics. The team wants to use managed AWS observability features and minimize custom instrumentation. Which operational management approach will BEST meet these requirements?
options: A) Configure CloudWatch dashboards and alarms for AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases Retrieve metrics only, and use ingestion job summary statistics to infer document status and chunk failures.
B) Configure CloudWatch dashboards and alarms for AWS/AOSS ingestion and search request metrics only, and use application request logs to infer Bedrock retrieval throttling and failures.

C) Configure CloudWatch dashboards and alarms for AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases Retrieve metrics and AWS/AOSS ingestion and search metrics, and enable knowledge base ingestion log delivery to inspect document status and chunk statistics.

D) Configure CloudWatch dashboards and alarms for AWS/AOSS StorageUsedInS3 and SearchOCU metrics, and compare StorageUsedInS3 with index size reports to validate document ingestion and logical index growth.
explanation: Three distinct layers need visibility — Bedrock's own Retrieve runtime, OpenSearch Serverless's indexing/search path, and per-document ingestion lifecycle — and each is covered by a different managed signal. C) AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases metrics catch Retrieve invocations/errors/throttles at the Bedrock layer; AWS/AOSS metrics separately expose OpenSearch Serverless indexing and search request health; knowledge base ingestion log delivery gives the per-document crawl/sync/index status plus chunk creation/deletion/failure statistics that no metric namespace provides — full coverage, all managed, no new instrumentation. A) Bedrock Retrieve metrics alone say nothing about OpenSearch Serverless indexing/search health, and ingestion job summary statistics don't give the per-document lifecycle detail or chunk statistics that ingestion logs provide. B) AOSS metrics alone miss Bedrock-layer Retrieve throttles/errors, and application logs only show symptoms, not the managed throttle/error signals themselves. D) StorageUsedInS3 reflects physical S3 storage (including replication/metadata overhead), not logical index size — it's not a reliable proxy for ingestion correctness or index growth.
domain: Domain 4 — Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
task: 4.3 — Implement monitoring systems for GenAI applications

question: A telemedicine provider's clinical documentation AI team operates an internal note-drafting service. The API layer is an Amazon API Gateway REST API, AWS Lambda calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API directly, and the Lambda function writes only unstructured error strings. Support engineers spend hours correlating reports of wrong output, validation exceptions, and latency spikes. The team must improve triage across prompt versions, model invocations, and API hops. The solution must avoid storing raw PHI in logs and must not introduce a separate observability data store. Which TWO actions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: A) Centralize AWS CloudTrail Lake queries for API Gateway, Lambda, and Bedrock events, then use the audit events as the primary source for prompt content, model response, and latency analysis.

B) Emit structured JSON logs from the Lambda function with a correlation ID, prompt version, model ID, sanitized prompt and response attributes, latency, validation outcome, and Bedrock request metadata; analyze the fields with CloudWatch Logs Insights queries.

C) Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging for full request and response payloads in CloudWatch Logs, then use CloudWatch Logs Insights queries to mask PHI values when engineers investigate incidents.

D) Enable X-Ray tracing on API Gateway and Lambda, instrument the Lambda AWS SDK client to create downstream Bedrock subsegments, and include the trace or correlation ID in the structured application logs.

E) Configure Amazon Bedrock agent tracing for preprocessing, orchestration, postprocessing, and guardrail traces, then use the traces to inspect every Lambda request without changing the direct FM invocation path.
explanation: Effective triage needs both searchable application-level facts and cross-service timing, while the PHI constraint means sanitizing BEFORE logging, not after. B) Structured JSON logs (correlation ID, prompt version, model ID, sanitized prompt/response attributes, latency, validation outcome, Bedrock request metadata) give CloudWatch Logs Insights stable, queryable fields, with sensitive content redacted/summarized at emission time rather than stored raw. D) X-Ray on API Gateway + Lambda + instrumented Bedrock SDK subsegments shows exactly where time is spent across the request chain; including the same correlation ID in logs lets engineers pivot between the trace timeline and the log-level diagnostic details. A) CloudTrail is built for API-activity auditing (who called what, when) — it isn't designed to serve as the primary source for prompt content, model responses, or quality-signal analysis. C) Full-payload invocation logging followed by query-time masking still means raw PHI was stored first — this is the exact anti-pattern the requirement rules out; sanitize before writing, not after. E) Bedrock agent tracing only applies to requests processed through Agents for Amazon Bedrock — this application calls Converse directly from Lambda, so agent tracing wouldn't capture this path at all.
domain: Domain 2 — Implementation and Integration
task: 2.5 — Implement application integration patterns and development tools

question: A multi-step GenAI workflow processes user input through several prompts and transformations, passing intermediate JSON payloads between stages. Occasionally downstream steps fail because fields are missing, misnamed, or formatted incorrectly, and engineers struggle to trace which upstream prompt or transformation introduced the error. The GenAI development team wants to build observability and schema validation across the prompt pipeline so that format errors are detected early and debugging becomes easier. What do you recommend?
options: A) Skip explicit schema validation and instead log full JSON payloads after each stage to CloudWatch Logs, then leverage post-hoc analysis when errors appear. Use CloudWatch Metrics to track failure counts but do not enforce schema constraints up front.

B) Use AWS X-Ray to trace each stage in the workflow and log every intermediate JSON payload to CloudWatch Logs. Use downstream Lambda functions to handle malformed fields when errors occur. Configure Amazon SNS notifications only when final outputs fail validation.

C) Add AWS X-Ray tracing for each prompt and transformation, and manually inspect CloudWatch Logs when downstream failures occur. Use runtime error catching in the application to handle malformed JSON rather than pre-validation at each stage.

D) Instrument the workflow using AWS X-Ray to trace each prompt invocation and data transformation, and integrate JSON schema validation (for example using AWS Lambda or a custom validation layer) before each stage to enforce field names and types. Log validation failures in Amazon CloudWatch Logs and trigger Amazon SNS alerts when schema violations occur.
explanation: Tracing WHICH stage introduced an error requires validation gates AT EVERY stage boundary, not just at the end — otherwise malformed data silently propagates and the true origin gets lost. D) X-Ray traces every prompt invocation and transformation for precise stage-level visibility; JSON schema validation BEFORE EACH stage catches field-name/type/required-field violations immediately, at the exact point of origin, rather than letting them cascade; CloudWatch Logs plus SNS alerts give immediate, actionable feedback the moment a contract is broken — proactive gatekeeping, not reactive investigation. A) Logging full payloads without enforcing any schema constraints means malformed data still propagates freely — post-hoc analysis only starts AFTER the damage is done, and failure-count metrics alone give no insight into WHERE or WHY the schema broke. B) Deferring validation until the FINAL output allows malformed data to propagate across MULTIPLE prompts before being caught — this fails to isolate the root cause early, and alerting only on final-output failures misses upstream schema violations entirely. C) Tracing plus manual log inspection with only runtime error CATCHING (not pre-validation) is entirely reactive — downstream failures still occur, and engineers must manually sift through logs, which is slow and denies the pipeline any early gatekeeping on structure correctness.
domain: Domain 5 — Testing, Validation, and Troubleshooting
task: 5.2 — Troubleshoot GenAI applications
comparison_note: Different scope than AIPC01_D2_022's structured-logging + X-Ray pattern. D2_022 instruments a SINGLE Lambda-to-Bedrock call boundary — correlation IDs, sanitized prompt/response attributes, X-Ray subsegments for one hop, primarily for PHI-safe triage of wrong output/latency/validation issues in one integration. This question instruments a MULTI-STAGE pipeline where the goal is isolating WHICH of several sequential prompt/transformation stages introduced a schema break — the key added mechanism here is validation GATES between every stage (not just logging), so malformed data is caught and alerted on at its point of origin rather than propagating silently through the chain.

question: A medical imaging equipment manufacturer's service AI team is extending an FM-based troubleshooting assistant with MCP tools. The team will deploy the MCP server to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. One tool runs multi-step calibration simulations that can emit progress updates and can request missing parameter values during the same tool interaction. The team wants client integrations to remain portable across local testing and remote runtime invocation. Which implementation approach will meet these requirements?
options: A) Deploy a streamable-HTTP MCP server container to AgentCore Runtime, keep default stateless MCP handling, listen on 0.0.0.0:8000/mcp, and reuse Mcp-Session-Id values.
B) Deploy a streamable-HTTP MCP server container to AgentCore Runtime, configure stateful MCP handling, listen on 0.0.0.0:8000/mcp, and require Accept: application/x-ndjson.
C) Deploy a streamable-HTTP MCP server container to AgentCore Runtime, configure stateful MCP handling, listen on 0.0.0.0:8000/tools, and route MCP calls through a proxy.
D) Deploy a streamable-HTTP MCP server container to AgentCore Runtime, configure stateful MCP handling, listen on 0.0.0.0:8000/mcp, and use the official mcp client session.
explanation: Progress notifications and multi-turn elicitation within the same tool interaction require retained MCP session state, and AgentCore Runtime has a specific required endpoint contract plus a documented client pattern for portability. D) Stateful MCP handling preserves session state across the multi-step calibration tool's progress updates and parameter elicitation; listening on 0.0.0.0:8000/mcp matches exactly what AgentCore Runtime expects for MCP-protocol containers; using the official mcp package's ClientSession is the documented portable client pattern that works the same locally and against remote runtime invocation. A) Stateless is the documented default for simple independent calls, but it can't retain session state needed for elicitation/progress notifications across the same interaction. B) Correct server mode and path, but the Accept header must follow the MCP standard (application/json or text/event-stream) — application/x-ndjson isn't the documented standard header. C) Correct stateful mode, but the endpoint path is wrong — AgentCore Runtime requires 0.0.0.0:8000/mcp, not /tools, and routing through a proxy isn't the documented pattern.
domain: Domain 2 — Implementation and Integration
task: 2.1 — Implement agentic AI solutions and tool integrations

question: An online legal research provider's search AI team runs a customer-facing assistant by using Amazon Bedrock ConverseStream with a supported on-demand Claude model. Each request begins with the same long system instructions, citation rules, and jurisdiction taxonomy. The application then appends retrieved case snippets and the user's question, which vary for each request. Profiling shows that repeated processing of the shared prompt material is increasing initial response latency and input-token cost. The team wants to reduce latency and cost without changing models or building a separate response cache. Which caching configuration will meet these requirements?
options: A) Add cache checkpoints every 1,024 tokens throughout the full request, set each CachePointBlock type to default, and use the same checkpoint layout for every supported foundation model.
B) Add a Bedrock prompt cache checkpoint after the retrieved snippets and user question, keep the checkpoint ttl at 1h, and rely on Bedrock to reuse the earlier prompt material.
C) Move the workload to Amazon Bedrock batch inference, add CachePointBlock objects to each request payload, and use response streaming only for user-visible follow-up requests.

D) Add a Bedrock prompt cache checkpoint after the shared instructions, citation rules, and taxonomy, keep that prefix unchanged across requests, and verify it meets the model-specific minimum token count.
explanation: Bedrock prompt caching only reuses a static, unchanged, contiguous PREFIX — so the checkpoint has to sit exactly at the boundary between what's shared/repeated and what varies per request. D) Placing the checkpoint right after the shared instructions/citation rules/taxonomy (the truly static leading content), keeping that prefix byte-for-byte unchanged across requests, and confirming it meets the model-specific minimum token threshold is exactly how prompt caching is designed to be used — reducing both latency and input-token cost with no new cache infrastructure. A) A universal 1,024-token checkpoint cadence assumes one-size-fits-all limits, but Bedrock's prompt-cache minimums and checkpoint counts are model-specific — this isn't a valid cross-model strategy. B) Placing the checkpoint after the retrieved snippets and user question — the parts that change every request — means the 'cached' prefix itself changes each time, causing a cache miss instead of reuse; the checkpoint has to come BEFORE the varying content, not after it. C) Prompt caching is explicitly not supported with the Bedrock batch inference API — moving to batch inference abandons the documented caching path entirely, on top of not matching the interactive, streaming use case.
domain: Domain 4 — Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
task: 4.1 — Implement cost optimization and resource efficiency strategies

question: An airline loyalty program's contact-center AI team wants to decide whether to replace an existing non-Bedrock answer generator with an Amazon Bedrock model. The team has prepared 750 representative customer prompts in Amazon S3. For each prompt, the dataset includes the existing system's response with modelIdentifier set to legacy-assistant-v1. The team has 45 senior agents who must independently rate the legacy response and the candidate model response for helpfulness and preference. At least three agents should review each prompt, and the team wants an AWS-managed workflow with results stored in S3 for later analysis. Which approach meets these requirements with the least custom development?
options: A) Create an Amazon Bedrock human-based model evaluation job with the candidate model and a bring-your-own response source named production-baseline. Use the S3 prompt dataset and an S3 output location, choose a comparison rating method, and set three workers per prompt.

B) Create an Amazon Bedrock human-based model evaluation job with the candidate model, the legacy response source, and a control response source. Use the S3 prompt dataset and an S3 output location, choose a comparison rank method, and set three workers per prompt.

C) Create an Amazon Bedrock automatic model evaluation job with the candidate model and a bring-your-own response source named legacy-assistant-v1. Use the S3 prompt dataset and an S3 output location, choose a quality metric, and review the computed scores.

D) Create an Amazon Bedrock human-based model evaluation job with the candidate model and a bring-your-own response source named legacy-assistant-v1. Use the S3 prompt dataset and an S3 output location, choose a comparison rating method, and set three workers per prompt.
explanation: Subjective helpfulness/preference judgment from named human reviewers, comparing a candidate model against an existing non-Bedrock system's stored responses, maps directly to a Bedrock human-based evaluation job with a correctly-named bring-your-own response source. D) The bring-your-own source name (legacy-assistant-v1) exactly matches the modelIdentifier already in the dataset, so Bedrock can correctly attribute the existing responses; a comparison rating method with three workers per prompt gives independent human judgment on both helpfulness and preference; S3 in/out and the 750-prompt count are within documented limits. A) Naming the bring-your-own source 'production-baseline' instead of matching the dataset's actual modelIdentifier (legacy-assistant-v1) means Bedrock can't correctly identify which stored responses belong to the existing system. B) Human-based evaluation jobs support at most two inference sources — adding a third (candidate + legacy + control) exceeds the documented limit, even though ranking is a valid rating style otherwise. C) Automatic evaluation produces computed metrics only — it doesn't collect the required independent human ratings/preferences from the senior agents at all.
domain: Domain 5 — Testing, Validation, and Troubleshooting
task: 5.1 — Implement evaluation systems for GenAI
comparison_note: See AIPC01_D5_011 for the LLM-as-a-judge counterpart: unlike this human-based evaluation job's two-source limit, judge-based jobs support only ONE model response per prompt and one modelIdentifier per job — comparing multiple candidates there requires separate jobs.

question: An investment research publisher's AI governance team is validating a market commentary assistant before a production release. One candidate uses an Amazon Bedrock model, and another candidate runs outside Amazon Bedrock. For the external candidate, the team has already generated responses for a fixed prompt set with expert reference responses. The team needs an automated assessment that goes beyond lexical overlap by scoring qualities such as relevance, factual accuracy, helpfulness, and coherence; includes an explanation for each prompt and response; writes the full report to S3; and does not call the external model during evaluation. Which approach will meet these requirements?
options: A) Create LLM-as-a-judge model evaluation jobs with applicationType ModelEvaluation. Store both candidates' responses in one JSON Lines file with two modelResponses per prompt, select built-in judge metrics, and configure the S3 output destination.

B) Create RAG evaluation jobs with applicationType RagEvaluation. Store each candidate answer as retrieved context in the prompt dataset, select retrieve-only metrics, and configure the S3 output destination.

C) Create automatic model evaluation jobs with applicationType ModelEvaluation. Store the prompt dataset and external candidate responses as JSON Lines in S3, select one task type per job, and configure the S3 output destination.

D) Create LLM-as-a-judge model evaluation jobs with applicationType ModelEvaluation. Store the prompt dataset and the external candidate's single precomputed response per prompt as JSON Lines in S3, select built-in judge metrics, and configure the S3 output destination.
explanation: Qualitative, multi-dimensional, per-response-explained scoring of a precomputed EXTERNAL (non-Bedrock) model's answers is exactly LLM-as-a-judge model evaluation's designed scope, but the bring-your-own format has a strict one-response-per-prompt limit that shapes how the job must be structured. D) An LLM-as-a-judge job scores relevance/correctness/helpfulness/coherence with a per-prompt explanation, writes the full report to S3, and critically supports precomputed (bring-your-own) responses so the external model is never invoked during evaluation — with exactly one response per prompt and one modelIdentifier, matching the documented constraint. A) Packing TWO modelResponses per prompt into one dataset record violates the documented limit — a judge evaluation job supports only one response per prompt and one unique modelIdentifier per job; comparing multiple candidates requires separate jobs. B) RAG evaluation (RagEvaluation) targets knowledge base/RAG retrieval behavior, not standalone generated-answer comparison — treating generated answers as 'retrieved context' misuses the application type entirely. C) Automatic evaluation is task-based (BERTScore, F1, toxicity, robustness, RWK) and requires selecting one task type per job — it doesn't provide the qualitative judge explanations across multiple dimensions the requirement asks for.
domain: Domain 5 — Testing, Validation, and Troubleshooting
task: 5.1 — Implement evaluation systems for GenAI
comparison_note: Compare with AIPC01_D5_007 for a documented-limits contrast worth memorizing: human-based evaluation jobs support up to TWO bring-your-own/candidate inference sources per job (D5_007's scenario legitimately compares candidate vs. legacy in one job). LLM-as-a-judge model evaluation jobs support only ONE model response per prompt and one unique modelIdentifier per job — comparing multiple candidates (as this question's wrong answer A attempts) requires separate jobs, not one job with multiple responses packed in. Same underlying idea (bring-your-own precomputed responses so the source model isn't re-invoked), different per-evaluation-type limit on how many candidates one job can hold.

question: A maritime logistics firm's operations AI team runs an Amazon Bedrock assistant by using the Converse API through the bedrock-runtime endpoint. Each request contains small structured inputs and asks the model to return one of three short JSON decisions. During port congestion events, the workload receives token-based throttling even though most completed responses contain fewer than 150 tokens. The application sets maxTokens to 4,096 on every request to avoid truncation. The team must improve completed requests per minute while continuing to use the same model, the same Converse API integration, and on-demand throughput. Which action will MOST directly improve throughput under these constraints?
options: A) Enable response streaming for the existing Converse calls, and keep the 4,096-token ceiling for every request.
B) Use a cross-Region inference profile for the Converse calls, and keep the 4,096-token ceiling for every request.
C) Set task-specific maxTokens ceilings for the short JSON responses, and trim oversized prompt context before invocation.
D) Increase client-side concurrency for the Converse calls, and retry throttled requests with exponential backoff.
explanation: Bedrock reserves token quota at request START based on input tokens plus the CONFIGURED max_tokens ceiling, not the tokens actually generated — so an oversized maxTokens setting reserves far more capacity than a short-JSON task needs, throttling throughput even though actual usage is small. C) Right-sizing maxTokens to match the task's real bounded output (well under 4,096) plus trimming unnecessary prompt context directly shrinks the per-request reservation, letting more requests fit within the same on-demand quota — no model change, no provisioned throughput purchase. A) Streaming improves time-to-first-visible-output but doesn't touch the upfront quota reservation created by the oversized maxTokens value. B) Cross-Region inference profiles help distribute supported on-demand traffic across Regions but do nothing about the reservation size per request. D) More concurrency increases the number of simultaneous large reservations — this can make token-based throttling worse, not better; backoff retries only help tolerate throttling after it happens, they don't prevent the underlying over-reservation.
domain: Domain 4 — Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
task: 4.1 — Implement cost optimization and resource efficiency strategies

question: A maritime logistics provider's platform engineering team operates a centralized GenAI gateway that standardizes access to Amazon Bedrock prompts, guardrail checks, audit logging, and client throttling. Product teams submit prompt packages and gateway configuration through Git. The release process must run security, prompt regression, and guardrail integration tests before deployment, publish test results for each run, and automatically recover from a failed non-source deployment stage by returning to the last known good gateway configuration. The team wants to use native AWS CodePipeline and AWS CodeBuild capabilities with minimal custom orchestration and no unsupported rollback behavior. Which implementation will meet these requirements?
options: A) Create a CodePipeline with a source stage, a CodeBuild test action that emits secondary artifacts, and a deploy stage configured with both automatic retry and an onFailure rollback condition.

B) Create a CodePipeline with a source stage configured for automatic rollback, a CodeBuild test action that uploads JUnit reports to S3, and a deploy stage that always reuses the current source revision.

C) Create a CodePipeline with a source stage, a CodeBuild test action whose buildspec defines one to five report groups, and a deploy stage configured for automatic rollback after a successful baseline execution.
D) Create a CodePipeline with a source stage, a CodeBuild test action whose buildspec defines six report groups, and a deploy stage configured for automatic rollback after the first failed execution.
explanation: Native, supported CI/CD recovery requires staying inside documented limits for both test reporting and rollback semantics. C) A buildspec with one to five report groups is within CodeBuild's documented per-project limit and produces structured, published test results each run; a deploy stage with automatic rollback configured AFTER a successful baseline execution correctly uses CodePipeline's stage-level rollback, which requires a prior successful execution in that stage to roll back to. A) An onFailure condition can specify retry OR rollback as the result — not both simultaneously — so this configuration is invalid regardless of secondary artifacts. B) CodePipeline does not support rolling back a SOURCE stage at all — this relies on unsupported behavior, and 'always reuse the current source revision' doesn't implement the required rollback-to-last-known-good semantics either. D) Six report groups exceeds CodeBuild's documented one-to-five limit, and automatic rollback needs a prior SUCCESSFUL stage execution to roll back to — configuring rollback after the first FAILED execution has no known-good baseline to recover to.
domain: Domain 2 — Implementation and Integration
task: 2.3 — Design and implement enterprise integration architectures

question: A maritime insurance underwriter's claims AI platform team uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases for a RAG assistant. The team is tuning chunking and retrieval settings before connecting the retrieved content to a foundation model. The team needs a repeatable prerelease test that evaluates only the retrieval component against SME-written ground-truth answers, and the team also needs request-level troubleshooting for retrieval path latency without adding application-side timing code. Which approach best meets these requirements?
options: A) Create an S3 .jsonl prompt dataset with single-turn records that include prompt and referenceContexts. Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation with Builtin.ContextRelevance and Builtin.ContextCoverage. Use KnowledgeBases CloudWatch metrics for latency analysis.

B) Create an S3 .jsonl prompt dataset with single-turn records that include knowledgeBaseIdentifier and retrievedResults. Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation with Builtin.Correctness and Builtin.Completeness. Use model-runtime CloudWatch metrics for latency analysis.

C) Create an S3 .jsonl prompt dataset with single-turn records that include prompt and referenceResponses. Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation with Builtin.ContextRelevance and Builtin.ContextCoverage. Use AWS X-Ray traces for Retrieve latency analysis.

D) Create an S3 .jsonl prompt dataset with up to five-turn records that include prompt and referenceResponses. Run a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation with Builtin.Faithfulness and Builtin.CitationCoverage. Use KnowledgeBases CloudWatch metrics for latency analysis.
explanation: Isolating just the retrieval component (not generation) against ground truth, plus request-level latency troubleshooting with zero app-side instrumentation, requires the exact retrieve-only job configuration and X-Ray tracing. C) A single-turn .jsonl dataset with prompt + referenceResponses (the documented ground-truth field for Bedrock-invoked retrieve-only jobs) feeds Builtin.ContextRelevance and Builtin.ContextCoverage — metrics that evaluate retrieved content only, not generated answers; AWS X-Ray traces the Retrieve operation's internal steps and latency with no custom timing code needed. A) referenceContexts is only used for custom metrics on PRECOMPUTED retrieval datasets, not the standard ContextCoverage ground-truth field when Bedrock itself invokes the KB — and KnowledgeBases CloudWatch metrics don't provide the documented latency-tracing mechanism (that's X-Ray). B) Correctness/Completeness are retrieve-AND-generate metrics, not retrieve-only metrics, and model-runtime CloudWatch metrics measure FM invocation behavior, not KB retrieval troubleshooting. D) A retrieve-and-generate job evaluates both retrieval and generation together — it doesn't isolate the retrieval component as required, and KnowledgeBases CloudWatch metrics again aren't the documented latency-analysis path.
domain: Domain 5 — Testing, Validation, and Troubleshooting
task: 5.1 — Implement evaluation systems for GenAI
comparison_note: Useful pairing with AIPC01_D1_019 and AIPC01_D1_020 as a 'measure, then fix' sequence on the same underlying retrieval layer: this question is about correctly setting up a retrieve-only evaluation to MEASURE whether retrieval is returning good context (ContextRelevance/ContextCoverage against ground truth) before generation is even involved. D1_019 and D1_020 are about FIXING retrieval once a problem is identified — hybrid search + reranking for exact-identifier misses and poor ranking (D1_019), or query decomposition for multi-intent coverage gaps (D1_020). A realistic team would run something like this evaluation first, then apply the D1_019/D1_020-style fixes based on what the evaluation surfaces. Also compare with AIPC01_D5_009: that question is ad-hoc troubleshooting of a specific reported retrieval bug via the raw Retrieve operation's score/metadata fields — faster and more targeted than standing up a full retrieve-only evaluation job when you already suspect a specific ranking problem. It also reinforces that HYBRID search is only available for OpenSearch-Serverless-backed knowledge bases, not other custom vector stores like Pinecone. Also see AIPC01_D5_010, which uses the retrieve-AND-generate evaluation (not retrieve-only) specifically because the generation FM changed while retrieval stayed the same — a useful reminder that the evaluation type must match whichever component actually changed.

question: A legal research publisher's editorial AI team runs a RAG assistant on Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. The knowledge base is a custom knowledge base backed by a Pinecone vector store. After a large content migration, reviewers report that generated answers often cite paragraphs from the wrong jurisdiction. The team needs to determine whether the retrieval stage is returning poorly ranked chunks before changing prompts or generation settings. The team must keep the existing vector store during troubleshooting. Which approach will MOST directly isolate the retrieval problem?
options: A) Invoke the RetrieveAndGenerate operation and inspect the returned citations for each generated answer in the same fixed test prompt set.
B) Invoke the Retrieve operation with overrideSearchType set to HYBRID and compare the returned chunks against semantic-only results for the same prompt set.
C) Invoke the Retrieve operation with vectorSearchConfiguration metadata filters for jurisdiction and inspect only filtered chunks for the same prompt set.
D) Invoke the Retrieve operation with vectorSearchConfiguration and inspect retrievalResults content, metadata, location, and score for a fixed test prompt set.
explanation: Isolating retrieval quality from generation behavior means calling the operation that returns raw source chunks without invoking any FM, and inspecting the specific fields that reveal ranking problems. D) Retrieve (not RetrieveAndGenerate) returns retrievalResults with content, metadata, location, and score — score is documented as a relevancy score usable to diagnose ranking, letting the team see directly whether wrong-jurisdiction chunks are being retrieved or ranked too highly after the migration, with zero FM involvement. A) RetrieveAndGenerate couples retrieval with generation — a bad answer could come from retrieval, prompt construction, or model synthesis, so it doesn't isolate the retrieval stage as cleanly as raw Retrieve + score inspection. B) HYBRID search is only documented for an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store with a filterable text field — this knowledge base is Pinecone-backed, so HYBRID isn't an available override here; only semantic search applies to this custom vector store configuration. C) Pre-filtering by jurisdiction metadata would mask exactly the bug being investigated — whether UNFILTERED retrieval is ranking the wrong jurisdiction too highly — so filtering first defeats the diagnostic purpose.
domain: Domain 5 — Testing, Validation, and Troubleshooting
task: 5.2 — Troubleshoot GenAI applications
comparison_note: Complements AIPC01_D5_008 and AIPC01_D1_019 rather than conflicting with them. D5_008 is a formal, repeatable retrieve-only EVALUATION JOB (Builtin.ContextRelevance/ContextCoverage scored against SME ground truth) — a structured pre-release quality gate. This question is ad-hoc, request-level TROUBLESHOOTING of a specific reported bug using the raw Retrieve API's returned score/metadata/content fields directly — faster and more targeted when you already suspect a specific ranking problem (wrong jurisdiction) rather than running a full evaluation job. Also reinforces a fact from AIPC01_D1_019: HYBRID search override is only available for an OpenSearch-Serverless-backed knowledge base with a filterable text field — a Pinecone-backed (or other non-OpenSearch) custom vector store only supports semantic search, so HYBRID isn't a valid fix option there regardless of how well it would otherwise address the problem.

question: A medical device manufacturer's AI governance office already uses AWS Audit Manager for internal control evidence. The office is standardizing oversight for several FM applications that use Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker AI. The governance program must align with responsible AI principles, support automated and manually collected evidence, and avoid treating the assessment results as a formal compliance certification. Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom governance implementation?
options: A) Create an AWS Audit Manager assessment from the AWS Generative AI Best Practices Framework v1, collect automated evidence where supported, and attach manual evidence for procedural controls.
B) Create a custom AWS Audit Manager framework, define all responsible AI controls manually, and use application logs as the primary source for evidence collection.
C) Create Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for each application, collect intervention results during inference, and use blocked responses as the primary governance evidence.
D) Create an AWS Audit Manager assessment from the AWS Generative AI Best Practices Framework v2, collect automated evidence where supported, and attach manual evidence for procedural controls.
explanation: An AWS-managed governance framework that already spans responsible-AI principles and both Bedrock and SageMaker AI evidence collection is the least-custom path, provided the current supported version is used. D) The AWS Generative AI Best Practices Framework v2 supports automated evidence collection for both Bedrock and SageMaker AI plus manual evidence attachment for procedural controls (human review, policy approvals) — an organizational assessment tool, explicitly not a compliance certification. A) v1 is no longer supported for creating new assessments — using it fails the 'standardize new governance assessments' goal outright. B) A fully custom framework recreates control definitions the managed v2 framework already provides — significantly more governance implementation work than required. C) Guardrails are runtime safety controls (input/output filtering), not an organizational assessment framework — they don't provide the broader control sets, manual-evidence support, or SageMaker AI coverage the governance office needs.
domain: Domain 3 — AI Safety, Security, and Governance
task: 3.3 — Implement AI governance and compliance mechanisms
comparison_note: Sits one layer above AIPC01_D3_003 and AIPC01_D3_014 in the governance stack — those questions are about WHICH SPECIFIC ARTIFACTS constitute evidence for a given deployment (SageMaker Model Cards, Glue Data Catalog lineage, Bedrock invocation logging). This question is about the overarching ASSESSMENT FRAMEWORK an organization runs its evidence-collection program against (AWS Audit Manager + the AWS Generative AI Best Practices Framework). In practice these compose: the model cards, lineage metadata, and invocation logs from D3_003/D3_014 are exactly the kind of automated and manual evidence this framework-level assessment would collect.

question: An international architecture firm's AI platform team is launching several internal design-assistant applications on Amazon Bedrock. The firm is not an existing AWS Audit Manager customer. The governance board has approved a standard Bedrock guardrail that includes denied topics and sensitive information filters. Application teams invoke Bedrock directly from their own production roles by using Converse, ConverseStream, InvokeModel, and InvokeModelWithResponseStream. The board wants a control that prevents production callers from bypassing the approved guardrail during inference, while preserving the existing Bedrock runtime APIs and avoiding a custom proxy layer. Which approach best meets these requirements?
options: A) Create an AWS Audit Manager assessment from Generative AI Best Practices Framework v2, then use assessment evidence as the production approval mechanism.
B) Enable Bedrock model invocation logs for all production accounts, then review prompts and responses to identify teams that bypass the approved guardrail.
C) Publish the approved guardrail version and document it in the platform standards, then monitor application deployments for teams that omit the guardrail configuration.
D) Apply IAM policies to production Bedrock roles that require the approved bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier on supported runtime APIs, and require applications to pass the guardrail version.
explanation: A guardrail only applies to a call when the request itself references its identifier and version — so PREVENTING bypass (not just detecting it after the fact) requires making that reference mandatory at the authorization layer, without adding a proxy. D) An IAM policy condition on bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier makes authorization for the supported runtime APIs (Converse/ConverseStream/InvokeModel/InvokeModelWithResponseStream) DEPEND on the approved guardrail identifier+version being present in the request — direct callers literally cannot get authorized without it, preserving the native Bedrock invocation path with no custom proxy. A) The firm isn't an existing Audit Manager customer (and Audit Manager is no longer open to new customers), and even where usable, Audit Manager assessment evidence is explicitly documented as not verifying compliance or guaranteeing audit success — it's not a runtime enforcement mechanism at all. B) Invocation logging is reactive (after-the-fact review), not preventive — it can't stop a bypassing request, and enabled logs can even contain blocked content as plain text, requiring careful governance of their own. C) Publishing/documenting a standard doesn't force compliance — a caller can still omit the guardrail identifier and version unless something (like the IAM policy in D) actually blocks that at authorization time.
domain: Domain 3 — AI Safety, Security, and Governance
task: 3.1 — Implement input and output safety controls
comparison_note: Adds a new preventive-enforcement mechanism to the 'Guardrails alone is often sufficient' family (AIPC01_D3_001/D3_009/D3_013): those questions are about whether a single guardrail layer is enough coverage for a content-safety requirement. This question is about a different problem — making sure the approved guardrail actually gets USED on every production call, which the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier IAM condition key solves at the authorization layer. Also complements AIPC01_D3_017 (Audit Manager + the Generative AI Best Practices Framework): that question is the positive case for Audit Manager (an EXISTING customer using it for organizational evidence collection); this question is the negative case (not an existing customer, and Audit Manager wouldn't provide runtime enforcement even if it were usable) — together they mark Audit Manager's actual boundary of usefulness.

question: A regional energy utility's grid operations AI team runs a multi-tenant incident-analysis assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Each request can include a small alert or several pages of retrieved outage history, so requests per minute has not correlated with throttling or cost. The team needs to allocate per-tenant capacity before model invocation, defer work that would exceed each tenant's minute-level token budget, and avoid paying for capacity-estimation calls. Which approach will meet these requirements with the MOST accurate resource allocation?
options: A) Calculate tokens with a shared tokenizer library, combine the estimate with historical averages, and admit requests through per-tenant request-rate buckets.
B) Send requests directly with a reduced maxTokens value during busy periods, track throttling responses, and adjust per-tenant request-rate buckets afterward.
C) Call CountTokens for the selected model with the planned request shape, combine the estimate with the output limit, and admit requests through per-tenant token buckets.
D) Invoke a smaller Bedrock model to summarize each request, combine the summary length with the output limit, and admit requests through per-tenant token buckets.
explanation: The scarcity that matters here is TOKENS, not request counts (the scenario explicitly says RPM doesn't correlate with throttling/cost), and the estimate must be free and model-specific, taken before invocation. C) CountTokens is model-specific (matches the actual selected model's tokenization), free to call, and works from the planned request shape — combining that input estimate with the output limit gives an accurate upper-bound budget to check against per-tenant TOKEN buckets before ever invoking the model. A) A generic shared tokenizer doesn't match Bedrock's model-specific tokenization, and request-RATE buckets ignore the actual driver (variable prompt/context size), which the scenario explicitly flags as decoupled from request count. B) Reducing maxTokens controls output size but does nothing to estimate the (often much larger) input/context tokens before invocation, and throttling-based feedback is reactive, not a pre-invocation admission decision. D) Summarizing with a smaller model to estimate size still spends a real (costly) inference call before the admission decision — exactly the 'avoid paying for capacity-estimation calls' requirement this violates — and the summary length doesn't accurately represent the original request's token usage on the actual selected model.
domain: Domain 4 — Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
task: 4.2 — Optimize application performance
comparison_note: Reinforces the same 'CountTokens is free — use it before invoking' pattern seen in AIPC01_D4_002, applied to a different use case. D4_002 uses CountTokens to decide whether to PRUNE conversation history/RAG chunks for a single request to avoid context-window overflow and cost. This question uses CountTokens for MULTI-TENANT ADMISSION CONTROL — deciding whether to admit or defer an entire request against a tenant's minute-level token budget. Same free pre-invocation estimation tool, different scope of decision (shrink this request vs. gate this request). Also see AIPC01_D2_037 for a coarser variant of this same principle: API Gateway request validation/mapping templates for a fast, upfront SIZE-based gate — sufficient for simple boundary protection, versus this question's accurate CountTokens-based per-tenant budget check.

question: A generative AI platform exposes a public endpoint that accepts free-form user prompts and forwards them to a foundation model. During load testing, engineers observe that some requests fail unpredictably when users submit very long prompts or request verbose outputs. These failures cause retries at the client layer and increase overall latency. The development team wants to introduce controls so that requests exceeding safe limits are handled consistently before reaching the model. The solution must protect downstream services, provide predictable behavior for clients, and avoid embedding complex logic into application code. What do you recommend as the MOST operationally efficient solution for this workload?
options: A) Use AWS Lambda to calculate token usage for every request after it passes through the API layer. Truncate inputs and outputs dynamically based on remaining context window size. Allow the API to accept all requests without validation to maximize flexibility.

B) Use Amazon API Gateway to forward all requests to the backend and rely on the foundation model to return token limit errors. Capture those errors in AWS Lambda and retry the request with reduced parameters. Return the retried response to the client.

C) Use Amazon API Gateway to enforce payload size limits and additionally implement custom token counting logic in Lambda to dynamically rewrite prompts and outputs, truncate content when limits are exceeded, and retry requests automatically until they succeed, while logging all adjustments for audit purposes.

D) Use Amazon API Gateway request validation and mapping templates to enforce maximum input size and estimated token limits before invoking the backend. Reject requests that exceed configured thresholds with clear error responses. Forward only validated requests to the model invocation layer.
explanation: Predictable client behavior and downstream protection both point to rejecting oversized requests at the API BOUNDARY, before any backend resource is consumed — declaratively, not via custom truncation/retry logic. D) API Gateway request validation and mapping templates enforce max input size/estimated token thresholds before the backend is ever invoked; requests exceeding limits get a clear, immediate error response — fast, predictable, and centralizes token-limit logic declaratively rather than embedding it in application code. A) Calculating tokens in Lambda AFTER the API layer means the request has already consumed resources before being rejected — and accepting everything at the API layer removes the one control point that could stop it early; silent truncation can also produce misleading incomplete outputs without informing the client. B) Letting the model surface token-limit errors pushes the failure downstream — compute and latency are spent on a doomed invocation before the error returns, and retrying after failure only adds more latency/cost with inconsistent behavior under load. C) Custom dynamic prompt rewriting, truncation, and automatic retry-until-success in Lambda is real embedded complexity that obscures original user intent and masks genuine client issues — exactly what the requirement wants to avoid; enforcing limits early at the boundary is simpler and more effective.
domain: Domain 2 — Implementation and Integration
task: 2.4 — Implement FM API integrations
comparison_note: Related to AIPC01_D4_012 but at a coarser precision level. D4_012 uses Bedrock's CountTokens API for an ACCURATE, model-specific token count before invocation — needed there for per-tenant token-BUDGET admission control. This question uses API Gateway request validation and mapping templates for a coarser, faster upfront SIZE/estimated-token gate — sufficient when the goal is simply rejecting obviously-oversized requests with a clear error before they reach the backend, rather than precisely metering token budgets per caller. Both share the same core principle — validate and reject BEFORE invoking the model, not after — just at different levels of precision and for different purposes (coarse boundary protection vs. precise per-tenant budgeting).

question: A municipal tax software provider runs a nightly generative AI classification workload on Amazon SageMaker AI. The workload reads millions of small JSON Lines records from Amazon S3 and writes the classification results back to Amazon S3. The current transform job sends one record per container request on GPU instances, and monitoring shows low GPU utilization even though GPU memory has significant headroom. The model container can process newline-delimited batches and return one result per input record. The provider wants the job to finish faster while keeping the existing offline processing pattern. Which change will meet these requirements with the LEAST architectural change?
options: A) Deploy a SageMaker Asynchronous Inference endpoint, submit each S3 record as an invocation, and collect the generated outputs in Amazon S3.
B) Configure SageMaker Batch Transform to keep one record per request, increase the instance count, and keep per-instance concurrency unchanged.
C) Deploy a SageMaker real-time endpoint with target tracking scaling, invoke it from parallel Lambda workers, and store responses in Amazon S3.
D) Configure SageMaker Batch Transform to use MultiRecord batching, increase MaxConcurrentTransforms, and tune MaxPayloadInMB for the container.
explanation: Low GPU utilization with headroom on small independent records signals a per-request-overhead problem, not a raw capacity problem — the fix is tuning Batch Transform's own batching/concurrency knobs, not adding infrastructure. D) MultiRecord batching sends multiple records per container request (since the container supports newline-delimited batches), MaxConcurrentTransforms raises how many requests hit each instance in parallel, and MaxPayloadInMB is tuned to fit more records per request — together these raise per-instance GPU utilization and throughput within the same offline, S3-based Batch Transform pattern, the smallest architectural change possible. A) Async Inference adds endpoint and invocation-queue management for a finite job that already works fine as batch — it doesn't optimize the existing batch path, it replaces it. B) More instances with unchanged one-record-per-request behavior and unchanged concurrency just parallelizes the same underutilization across more (costlier) instances — it doesn't fix the root per-instance inefficiency. C) A real-time endpoint is built for low-latency online serving, not a finite nightly batch job — adding Lambda-driven parallel invocation is real orchestration overhead that bypasses Batch Transform's purpose-built batching controls entirely.
domain: Domain 4 — Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
task: 4.2 — Optimize application performance
comparison_note: Don't confuse with AIPC01_D4_007's 'Bedrock batch inference' — they're different services solving superficially similar-sounding 'batch/offline processing' problems. D4_007 is about a Bedrock FOUNDATION MODEL workload (nightly transcript summarization via Amazon Bedrock's own batch inference API — prompts to S3, batch job, results to S3). This question is about a SAGEMAKER-HOSTED custom model workload (a classification container on SageMaker AI, tuned via SageMaker Batch Transform's BatchStrategy/MaxConcurrentTransforms/MaxPayloadInMB settings). If the model is invoked through Amazon Bedrock → Bedrock batch inference is the relevant offline mechanism; if the model is a container/endpoint hosted on SageMaker AI → SageMaker Batch Transform tuning is the relevant mechanism — the underlying AWS services and configuration knobs are completely different even though both are 'batch inference.'

question: A precision agriculture equipment manufacturer's connected-equipment AI team is choosing Amazon Bedrock foundation models for a field-support assistant. The assistant must answer text questions, stream responses to mobile clients, call application tools when needed, run in approved production Regions, and avoid models that could create near-term migration risk. Executives want a defensible selection process that weighs business quality, operational fit, and cost instead of relying only on public benchmark rankings. Which TWO actions should the team take to select foundation models that best align with these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: A) Run a latency and token-cost bakeoff by using Converse-compatible prompts for models with tool use, then prioritize the fastest acceptable response profile.
B) Run Bedrock evaluation jobs on representative prompt datasets, then compare evaluation results with measured latency, throughput needs, and pricing for the shortlisted models.
C) Use ListFoundationModels as the only selection source, then rank candidates by context window, service tier, quotas, and model-specific inference parameters.
D) Use public benchmark results and Bedrock model cards to seed a shortlist, then choose the lowest priced model that supports text output and streaming.
E) Build a candidate matrix from Bedrock model documentation and discovery APIs that compares modalities, API support, Region availability, inference types, and lifecycle status.
explanation: Defensible FM selection needs a comprehensive operational-fit matrix PLUS workload-specific quality evidence — not a single-dimension shortcut like price, benchmark rank, or one API call. E) A candidate matrix built from Bedrock model documentation and discovery APIs covering modalities, API/streaming/tool-use support, Region availability, inference types, and lifecycle status (Active/Legacy/EOL) directly avoids migration risk and confirms production-fit constraints. B) Bedrock evaluation jobs on representative prompts give actual workload-specific quality evidence, which combined with measured latency/throughput/pricing supports a genuinely balanced business+technical decision — not reliance on public benchmarks that may not generalize. A) A latency/cost bakeoff alone is a valid operational signal but skips quality validation, Region/lifecycle checks, and other compatibility constraints — it's incomplete on its own. C) ListFoundationModels is useful for discovery but doesn't return every needed field (full catalog details, quotas, service tiers, complete parameter guidance) — treating it as the ONLY source misses real constraints. D) Benchmarks + model cards to shortlist is fine as a starting point, but picking the cheapest model meeting only basic text+streaming skips workload-specific quality testing and ignores tool-use support, Region approval, and lifecycle risk entirely.
domain: Domain 1 — Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
task: 1.2 — Select and configure FMs

question: A precision agriculture startup's platform team is exposing existing diagnostic tools to autonomous agents by using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. The tools are implemented in one shared AWS Lambda function, which currently dispatches to internal handlers by unprefixed names such as getSoilStatus and scheduleIrrigation. The team wants the tools to be MCP-compatible through Gateway, keep the existing handler names, and add defensive parameter validation in the Lambda code. Which implementation will meet these requirements with the least custom integration code?
options: A) Create an AgentCore Gateway Lambda target with the Lambda ARN and a toolSchema that defines each tool. In the Lambda dispatcher, validate the event fields and route directly by bedrockAgentCoreToolName after registering handlers with Gateway-visible names.

B) Create an AgentCore Gateway OpenAPI target from a Swagger 2.0 document that describes the Lambda operations. In the Lambda dispatcher, map operationId values to handlers and validate request bodies after invocation.

C) Create an AgentCore Gateway Lambda target with the Lambda ARN and outputSchema definitions for each tool. In the Lambda dispatcher, read tool arguments from the context metadata and route directly by bedrockAgentCoreToolName.

D) Create an AgentCore Gateway Lambda target with the Lambda ARN and a toolSchema that defines each tool. In the Lambda dispatcher, validate the event fields from each inputSchema and strip the Gateway target-name prefix from bedrockAgentCoreToolName before selecting the handler.
explanation: Exposing an existing Lambda's unprefixed handler names as MCP tools through Gateway requires knowing exactly how Gateway names and delivers tool calls to that Lambda. D) A Lambda target with lambdaArn + toolSchema (required fields: name, description, inputSchema) is the documented way to register the tools; the Lambda event delivers inputSchema properties as values, so validating against each inputSchema is the right place for defensive checks; and because Gateway-visible tool names are prefixed as ${target_name}___${tool_name}, stripping that prefix before dispatch is what lets the shared Lambda keep its existing unprefixed handler names unchanged. A) Requiring handlers to be registered with Gateway-visible (prefixed) names couples the dispatcher to the prefix instead of preserving the existing unprefixed names — backwards from the requirement. B) Gateway OpenAPI targets support OpenAPI 3.0/3.1, not Swagger 2.0, and this approach doesn't use the documented Lambda target configuration for directly exposing an existing Lambda. C) outputSchema is optional, not what routes arguments — inputSchema properties arrive in the event object, not context metadata — and this option also fails to handle the tool-name prefix.
domain: Domain 2 — Implementation and Integration
task: 2.1 — Implement agentic AI solutions and tool integrations

question: A university admissions office's AI platform team is standardizing retrieval access for several admissions assistants. The team uses Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases as the retrieval source. Some assistants are MCP-compatible agents, while other assistants use Amazon Bedrock chat-style model integrations. The platform must provide a consistent retrieval tool interface, prevent application developers from passing knowledge base identifiers at runtime, and support both single-pass retrieval and multi-step retrieval for complex questions with minimal custom code. Which implementation will best meet these requirements?
options: A) Create Converse API tool definitions for the retrieval operations, mirror the MCP-visible tool names in toolConfig, and have the model execute the retrieval calls directly.
B) Create a custom MCP server that wraps RetrieveAndGenerate, bind the managed knowledge base mapping in server configuration, and route every request through one retrieval-and-generation operation.

C) Create a Lambda-backed MCP gateway that calls Retrieve for every query, bind the managed knowledge base mapping in Lambda configuration, and rely on knowledge base guardrails for retrieved references.

D) Create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway target with the managed knowledge base connector, bind the managed knowledge base and retrieval settings to the target, and have clients invoke the target-prefixed Retrieve and AgenticRetrieveStream tools.
explanation: A consistent retrieval interface usable by both MCP agents and Bedrock chat-style integrations, with the KB ID hidden from application developers and both single-pass and multi-step retrieval supported, is exactly the managed knowledge base connector's designed scope. D) An AgentCore Gateway target with the managed KB connector binds the KB identifier and retrieval settings to the target itself — clients invoke the target-prefixed Retrieve (single-pass) and AgenticRetrieveStream (multi-step agentic) MCP tools without ever passing a knowledge base ID at runtime; both consumer types (MCP agents and chat-style integrations that can call MCP tools) get one consistent interface. A) The standard Bedrock tool-use pattern has the model REQUEST a tool call while application code executes it and returns a toolResult — 'the model executes the retrieval calls directly' misdescribes that pattern, and Converse tool names have documented constraints that make blindly mirroring MCP-visible prefixed names risky. B) RetrieveAndGenerate bundles retrieval with generation and citations into ONE operation — it doesn't expose separate single-pass vs multi-step retrieval tools, and a custom wrapper adds real maintenance and session-handling burden (including reusing the service-generated session ID). C) Retrieve alone provides only single-pass retrieval, not the multi-step agentic retrieval needed for complex questions, and knowledge base guardrails don't filter retrieved references at runtime — they act on input/generated response, not the retrieval-reference stream itself.
domain: Domain 1 — Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
task: 1.5 — Design retrieval mechanisms for FM augmentation
comparison_note: Part of the AgentCore family alongside AIPC01_D2_023 (AgentCore Runtime hosting a stateful MCP server) and AIPC01_D2_027 (AgentCore Gateway Lambda target exposing an existing Lambda's tools). Keep the AgentCore surface straight: Runtime hosts your own MCP server code; Gateway turns existing resources (Lambda functions, APIs, or — as in this question — a managed Knowledge Base) into MCP tools without you writing a server at all. This question's wrong-answer B is also a fresh instance of the recurring Retrieve-vs-RetrieveAndGenerate family (see AIPC01_D1_020's note): RetrieveAndGenerate bundles retrieval+generation into one call, so it can't expose the separate single-pass/multi-step retrieval TOOLS this platform requirement needs.

question: A global architecture firm's design-knowledge team stores building codes, project standards, and design-review notes as unstructured files in Amazon S3. The team is building a RAG assistant with Amazon Bedrock. The solution must use a managed Knowledge Bases ingestion path that parses documents, chunks content, creates embeddings, and writes those embeddings to a supported vector index. The platform team has no existing vector database service, wants to minimize new operational ownership, and wants the initial design to remain production ready while the source repository stays in S3. Which approach will BEST meet these requirements?
options: A) Create an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with an Amazon S3 data source and a MONGO_DB_ATLAS storage configuration for a vector index.
B) Create an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with a custom data source that reads the S3 objects and an OPENSEARCH_SERVERLESS storage configuration.
C) Create an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with an Amazon S3 data source and an RDS storage configuration for a dedicated vector index.
D) Create an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with an Amazon S3 data source and an OPENSEARCH_SERVERLESS storage configuration for a dedicated vector index.
explanation: The documents already live in S3 (a directly-supported connector) and the team explicitly has no existing vector database to operate, so the answer needs the simplest supported source + the storage type requiring the least new operational ownership.
