D) An S3 data source keeps ingestion architecture simple since it's a native supported connector; OPENSEARCH_SERVERLESS is a fully managed vector store option that doesn't require provisioning/operating a separate database platform — matching 'minimize new operational ownership' for an initial production-ready release. A) MONGO_DB_ATLAS is a valid Knowledge Bases vector store type technically, but it introduces an EXTERNAL platform the team has no existing service for — exactly the new operational ownership being avoided. B) A custom data source adds unnecessary integration work when the documents already reside in the natively-supported S3 connector — no reason to build a custom source here. C) RDS is a valid vector store type, but it introduces relational database infrastructure decisions (provisioning, patching, scaling) that OpenSearch Serverless avoids by being fully managed.
domain: Domain 1 — Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
task: 1.4 — Design and implement vector store solutions

question: A maritime logistics company's operations AI team runs an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases RAG application that uses an Amazon S3 data source containing port regulations, vessel handling procedures, and safety bulletins. The S3 objects are updated by multiple upstream systems throughout the day. The team must keep the vector store current, minimize unnecessary embedding-model usage, detect failed refreshes, and avoid creating a second source of truth outside the S3 bucket. Which combination of steps should the team implement? (Select TWO.)
options: A) Delete and recreate the knowledge base vector store on a schedule to guarantee that all removed and changed objects disappear.
B) Submit changed S3 documents by using direct document ingestion and run periodic data source syncs to reconcile the bucket later.
C) Modify only metadata sidecar files for CSV content when tags change so the next refresh avoids re-ingesting the documents.
D) Run a refresh workflow that starts a data source ingestion job for the knowledge base after source changes are published.
E) Track each refresh workflow until the ingestion job reaches a terminal successful status before marking the update complete.
explanation: Keeping S3 as the single source of truth while minimizing embedding-model usage and detecting failures means using the documented incremental sync workflow and actually watching it to completion. D) Starting a data source ingestion job after source changes are published triggers Bedrock's incremental sync — it only processes added/modified/deleted documents since the last sync, not the whole corpus, directly minimizing unnecessary embedding calls. E) Polling StartIngestionJob's returned ingestionJobId with GetIngestionJob until it reaches a terminal successful status is exactly how failures get detected and how downstream processes avoid assuming re-indexing finished when it didn't. A) Deleting and recreating the vector store on a schedule is unnecessary overhead — incremental sync already handles removed/changed objects without a full rebuild. B) Mixing direct document ingestion with periodic S3 syncs for the same data source creates drift, since directly-indexed changes aren't reflected back into the S3 bucket — exactly the 'second source of truth' problem the requirement wants to avoid. C) Metadata-only sidecar optimization doesn't apply to CSV files — updating a CSV's metadata file still triggers re-ingestion of the associated CSV.
domain: Domain 1 — Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
task: 1.4 — Design and implement vector store solutions

question: A healthcare provider manages a large library of patient education material that is frequently revised based on new clinical guidance, regulatory updates, and quality reviews. Some updates involve minor text edits that should trigger lightweight incremental updates to the vector store, while more urgent corrections must update embeddings immediately to avoid distributing outdated information to patients. Additionally, the provider requires a complete vector index rebuild every quarter to eliminate drift, fragmentation, and outdated embeddings. What maintenance architecture should the team deploy to keep the vector store current? (Select two)
options: A) Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with a quarterly document sync job for full index rebuild.
B) Use an hourly AWS Batch job to reprocess all documents and regenerate embeddings, with manual triggers for urgent updates.
C) Use Amazon EventBridge rules and AWS Lambda to process incremental updates and real-time corrections.
D) Use Amazon OpenSearch Service ingestion pipelines for all changes and rely on scheduled cron based reprocessing for full index replacement.
E) Use an EventBridge scheduled rule and an AWS Step Functions workflow to perform quarterly full index rebuilds.
explanation: Three distinct update cadences — lightweight incremental edits, urgent immediate corrections, and quarterly full rebuilds — need two complementary event-driven mechanisms, not one uniform batch/cron process. C) EventBridge rules triggering Lambda give an event-driven path for both lightweight incremental updates AND urgent real-time corrections — document-change events (from S3 or the application) fire immediately, propagating fixes fast without a full rebuild. E) An EventBridge SCHEDULED rule reliably triggers the quarterly cadence, and Step Functions orchestrates the multi-step process (extract all documents, regenerate embeddings, rebuild the index) needed to eliminate drift and fragmentation — a heavier, less-frequent workflow appropriately separated from the lightweight incremental path. A) Bedrock Knowledge Bases with quarterly sync REPLACES the existing custom vector store architecture with a different product entirely — it doesn't provide the maintenance architecture requested for the current vector index, and misses the incremental/urgent-correction tiers. B) Hourly full reprocessing of ALL documents is inefficient and doesn't provide either true lightweight incremental updates or truly immediate urgent corrections — manual triggers add operational delay and risk. D) Cron-based scheduled reprocessing for full replacement applies uniform processing regardless of urgency — it doesn't differentiate real-time corrections from routine incremental changes from quarterly full rebuilds, missing the tiered cadence the scenario requires.
domain: Domain 1 — Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
task: 1.4 — Design and implement vector store solutions
comparison_note: A different maintenance architecture than AIPC01_D1_027, and the choice between them depends on which vector store platform is actually in use. D1_027 is specifically about maintaining a Bedrock MANAGED Knowledge Base — its documented incremental sync mechanism is StartIngestionJob/GetIngestionJob, and the scenario there is entirely built around that Bedrock-native workflow. This question is about maintaining a CUSTOM (non-Bedrock-managed) vector store — hence the EventBridge + Lambda (incremental/urgent) + EventBridge scheduled rule + Step Functions (quarterly rebuild) pattern, and switching to Bedrock Knowledge Bases is explicitly the WRONG answer here because it changes the underlying platform rather than providing a maintenance architecture for the existing one. Same underlying goal (keep a vector store current across multiple update cadences), different toolchain depending on whether the vector store is Bedrock-managed or custom.

question: A global media streaming platform's personalization team operates an Amazon Bedrock FM feature that uses Converse and ConverseStream through the bedrock-runtime endpoint in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. The team must build observability that supports operational dashboards for latency, token use, throttles, errors, and streaming responsiveness. The team also must preserve forensic records with per-request product, tenant, and experiment identifiers. Logs must remain in the same account and Region where inference occurs, and the team wants to avoid parsing attribution values from prompt text. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: A) Create CloudWatch dashboards and alarms from CloudTrail API events for invocation volume, latency, token counts, errors, throttles, and TimeToFirstToken.
B) Create CloudWatch dashboards and alarms from AWS/Bedrock runtime metrics for invocation volume, latency, token counts, errors, throttles, and TimeToFirstToken.
C) Export AWS/Bedrock metrics from both Regions to a central dashboard, and use the metric records as the forensic source for prompts, responses, and attribution.
D) Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging in each inference Region to CloudWatch Logs or S3, and send attribution values by using requestMetadata.
E) Record product, tenant, and experiment IDs in application logs with Bedrock request IDs, and correlate those logs to invocation records during investigations.
explanation: Two distinct observability layers are needed — structured operational metrics for dashboards, and invocation-level records with attribution for forensic investigation — and each has its own documented mechanism. B) AWS/Bedrock runtime metrics natively cover invocation volume, latency, token counts, errors, throttles, and TimeToFirstToken — structured operational signals, no prompt parsing needed. D) Model invocation logging must be explicitly enabled per account/Region (destinations must be same account/Region as inference), and requestMetadata is the documented caller-supplied field for per-request product/tenant/experiment attribution inside Converse/ConverseStream invocation records — no need to infer attribution from prompt text. A) CloudTrail is API-activity audit, not the native runtime metrics stream — it doesn't replace AWS/Bedrock metrics for latency/token/throttle dashboards. C) AWS/Bedrock metrics are aggregated operational signals, not invocation payload records — they don't carry prompts, responses, or requestMetadata, so they can't serve as the forensic source. E) Recording IDs only in application logs doesn't populate the documented requestMetadata field inside Bedrock's own invocation log records — it adds correlation complexity instead of using the native per-request attribution mechanism.
domain: Domain 4 — Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
task: 4.3 — Implement monitoring systems for GenAI applications

question: A professional sports league's fan engagement AI team runs a public chatbot on Amazon Bedrock by calling the InvokeModel API directly from a backend service. The service builds each prompt from fixed system instructions, retrieved league policy content, and a free-form fan question. Recent red-team tests show attempts to override the system instructions, reveal hidden prompt text, and bypass safety behavior. The team wants runtime defenses that use managed Bedrock capabilities where possible and that block adversarial user input before it reaches the model. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: A) Configure the stored guardrail content policy with a Standard tier PROMPT_ATTACK filter, set an appropriate inputStrength, and set inputAction to BLOCK.
B) Run adversarial prompt test cases in Step Functions during release validation, and send production prompts without guardContent tags.
C) Specify the configured guardrail identifier and version on each InvokeModel request, and wrap the fan question in Bedrock guardContent input tags.
D) Configure denied topics and word filters in the guardrail, and rely on those filters to classify prompt injection attempts.
E) Redact PII from the fan question with Amazon Comprehend, and rely on the redacted prompt to prevent jailbreak behavior.
explanation: Blocking jailbreaks, injection, and prompt leakage with a managed control requires the specific PROMPT_ATTACK filter type (not generic content filters) and correctly wiring it into an InvokeModel call, which has stricter requirements than Converse. A) The PROMPT_ATTACK content policy filter is Bedrock's documented mechanism for jailbreak/injection/leakage detection; prompt leakage detection specifically requires the Standard tier, and inputAction BLOCK stops matching input before it reaches the model. C) For InvokeModel/InvokeModelWithResponseStream, the guardrail identifier+version must be specified on the request AND the user-controlled text must be wrapped in guardContent tags — without those tags, prompt attack filtering isn't applied to that input even if a guardrail exists. B) Adversarial testing in Step Functions is valuable pre-release validation, but it's not a runtime blocking control, and sending prompts without guardContent tags means filtering won't apply to live traffic anyway. D) Denied topics/word filters are for content-policy enforcement, not the documented prompt-injection/jailbreak detection mechanism — that specifically requires the PROMPT_ATTACK filter. E) PII redaction addresses a different risk (privacy) entirely and doesn't classify or block jailbreak/injection/leakage attempts.
domain: Domain 3 — AI Safety, Security, and Governance
task: 3.1 — Implement input and output safety controls
comparison_note: Deepens the 'Guardrails alone is often sufficient for a simple input-safety requirement' pattern seen in AIPC01_D3_001/D3_009/D3_013, but at a much more technical level: this question isn't testing WHETHER Guardrails alone suffices (no defense-in-depth language here either, so it would), it's testing the EXACT configuration mechanics needed to make Guardrails actually work for adversarial-input detection specifically — the PROMPT_ATTACK filter type (not generic topic/word filters), the Standard tier requirement for leakage detection, and the guardContent tagging requirement that's easy to miss when calling InvokeModel directly instead of Converse. Also see AIPC01_D3_021, which introduces Prompt Attack set to DETECT (for a monitoring/observation period before enforcement) as a contrast to this question's BLOCK-for-immediate-enforcement configuration.

question: A digital banking platform's conversational AI team runs a customer-facing assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Red-team testing found harmful language in both user prompts and generated responses, plus jailbreak and prompt leakage attempts. Compliance requires blocking harmful content when the guardrail classification is MEDIUM or HIGH, but allowing LOW classifications to reduce false positives. The team also needs to observe prompt attack detections for 30 days before changing user-visible behavior, and must anonymize PII in text responses. Which configuration will meet these requirements?
options: A) Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail in the Standard tier. Set Hate, Insults, Sexual, Violence, and Misconduct filters to Low for prompts and responses, set Prompt Attack to Block, and set sensitive information filters to Mask.

B) Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail in the Standard tier. Set Hate, Insults, Sexual, Violence, and Misconduct filters to High for prompts and responses, add jailbreaks as denied topics, and set sensitive information filters to Block.

C) Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail in the Standard tier. Set Hate, Insults, Sexual, Violence, and Misconduct filters to Medium for prompts only, set Prompt Attack to Block, and configure word filters for PII values.

D) Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail in the Standard tier. Set Hate, Insults, Sexual, Violence, and Misconduct filters to Medium for prompts and responses, set Prompt Attack to Detect, and set sensitive information filters to Mask.
explanation: Every requirement maps to a specific filter STRENGTH or ACTION setting, and mismatching either produces the wrong behavior even with the right feature enabled. D) Medium filter strength blocks MEDIUM and HIGH classifications while allowing LOW through — exactly the compliance/false-positive balance requested, applied to both prompts AND responses (harmful content was found in both); Prompt Attack set to Detect returns detections in the trace without changing user-visible behavior — the correct mechanism for a 30-day observation period before enforcement; sensitive information filters set to Mask anonymizes PII with tags rather than blocking the whole response, preserving utility. A) Low strength blocks only HIGH classifications — MEDIUM harmful content would pass through, failing compliance; Prompt Attack set to Block changes user-visible behavior immediately, which is the opposite of an observation period. B) High strength blocks LOW, MEDIUM, and HIGH — stricter than the stated tolerance, increasing false positives; Block on sensitive information filters replaces content with a blocked message rather than anonymizing via Mask. C) Filtering prompts ONLY misses harmful model RESPONSES, part of the stated risk; word filters are not the same mechanism as sensitive information filters for PII; and Block on Prompt Attack again fails the observation-period requirement.
domain: Domain 3 — AI Safety, Security, and Governance
task: 3.1 — Implement input and output safety controls
comparison_note: Deepens two configuration-mechanics threads already in the bank. First, AIPC01_D3_019 uses Prompt Attack set to BLOCK for immediate enforcement — this question introduces DETECT mode specifically for a monitoring/observation period before enforcement changes user-visible behavior, a distinction D3_019 didn't need to test. Second, this question's sensitive-information-filters=Mask setting reinforces the Mask-for-anonymization-vs-Block-for-full-removal distinction that AIPC01_D3_020/AIPC01_D3_002 rely on for PII handling — Mask preserves utility (placeholders, still usable text) where Block would remove content entirely.

question: A luxury hotel chain's guest experience platform team is enhancing its CRM with a generative AI summary for each guest-service interaction. The CRM integration writes a compact event containing the interaction ID and transcript pointer to an Amazon SQS queue. A Lambda function calls Amazon Bedrock, writes the summary back to the CRM, and completes well within the Lambda timeout. The CRM API supports an idempotency key. Traffic arrives in bursts, summaries do not need to be returned to the original CRM request, and the team must minimize operational overhead while preventing duplicate CRM updates. Which implementation should the team use?
options: A) Invoke the Lambda function from the CRM webhook with InvocationType=RequestResponse. Return the generated summary through the CRM webhook response.
B) Invoke the Lambda function from the integration layer with InvocationType=Event. Write each generated summary to the CRM without an idempotency check.
C) Configure an Amazon SQS event source mapping for the Lambda function. Use the interaction ID as the idempotency key when writing the CRM summary.
D) Configure an Amazon SQS event source mapping for the Lambda function. Treat batch delivery semantics as sufficient to prevent duplicate CRM summary writes.
explanation: SQS event source mappings deliver at least once, not exactly once — so any external side effect (like a CRM write) triggered from that path must be made idempotent, not assumed safe by the queue mechanics alone. C) An SQS event source mapping fits the bursty, no-immediate-response-needed integration; using the stable interaction ID as the CRM's idempotency key means repeated processing of the same record converges on the same CRM update instead of creating duplicates — the correct fix at the actual point of risk. A) RequestResponse is synchronous and holds the webhook open until processing finishes — unnecessary coupling when no immediate response is required and a queue already exists to absorb bursts. B) Event invocation decouples the caller, but skipping the idempotency check ignores exactly the duplicate-write risk the requirement calls out — decoupling alone doesn't solve it. D) SQS event source mappings are documented as at-least-once delivery — assuming batch delivery alone prevents duplicates is unsafe; the same record can genuinely be processed more than once.

comparison_note: Loosely related to AIPC01_D2_002 — both use SQS + Lambda to decouple a producer from Bedrock processing and absorb bursts. D2_002's focus is the DECOUPLING itself: giving a legacy HTTPS-only on-prem system immediate acknowledgment while buffering bursts before Bedrock inference. This question assumes the decoupling is already in place and zeroes in on a different, easy-to-miss gotcha: SQS event source mappings are at-least-once, so any external side effect (a CRM write) triggered downstream must be made idempotent — decoupling with a queue does not, by itself, prevent duplicate processing.

question: A pharmaceutical clinical operations platform ingests partner trial-site notes as JSON into Amazon S3, normalizes them, and then creates embeddings for an Amazon Bedrock RAG application. The incoming JSON contains nested structs and lists, and the team must quarantine records that fail completeness and uniqueness checks before the curated dataset is loaded for embedding. The workflow must publish rule pass and fail counts to Amazon CloudWatch for alarms and minimize custom validation code. Which validation design best meets these requirements?
options: A) Build an AWS Glue ETL validation stage that reads the raw nested JSON, runs EvaluateDataQuality with a lowercase dqdl rules list, leaves default publishing options unchanged, and writes records with failed row percentages to quarantine.

B) Configure AWS Glue Data Quality in the Data Catalog after the ETL job writes the curated table, generate recommended completeness and uniqueness rules, enable scheduled evaluations, and quarantine records by interpreting failed-rule results.

C) Configure AWS Glue Data Quality in the Data Catalog on the raw JSON table, generate recommended rules for completeness and uniqueness, publish the catalog run results, and use the resulting score to quarantine failing records before embedding.

D) Build an AWS Glue ETL validation stage that flattens nested fields, uses EvaluateDataQuality.processRows or Glue Studio row-level output with case-sensitive DQDL, enables CloudWatch metrics, and splits pass and fail records for curated and quarantine writes.
explanation: Row-level quarantine BEFORE embedding, on nested JSON, with explicit CloudWatch metrics, requires the ETL entry point (not the Data Catalog entry point), correctly flattened data, case-sensitive DQDL, and explicitly enabled metrics publishing. D) The ETL job entry point supports proactive validation and filtering before data loads downstream; flattening nested structs/lists first is required since Glue Data Quality doesn't evaluate arbitrary nested/list sources directly; EvaluateDataQuality.processRows (or the Glue Studio row-level output) gives the actual row-level pass/fail split needed for quarantine; case-sensitive DQDL (capitalized Rules, IsComplete/IsUnique) is required syntax; CloudWatch metrics must be explicitly enabled since publishing defaults to off. A) DQDL is case-sensitive — a lowercase rules list is invalid — and leaving default CloudWatch publishing options unchanged means metrics still won't publish (defaults to disabled). B) Running Data Catalog evaluations AFTER the curated table is written happens too late to validate/filter records before the embedding dataset loads, and Data Catalog evaluations don't provide the failed-record identification needed for an automated quarantine workflow. C) The Data Catalog entry point is for evaluating cataloged datasets and recommending rules, not for identifying individual failed records in an ETL flow — its output is an aggregate score (percentage of rules passed), not a row-level pass/fail signal usable for quarantine decisions.

question: A document analysis system processes very large technical reports and feeds selected content into a foundation model to generate summaries and answers. As document size increases, engineers observe that some responses are incomplete or miss critical sections, especially when long inputs are passed through multi step workflows. Logs show that parts of the input are not consistently reaching the model during peak usage. The team wants to redesign how documents are split and passed to the model so that important context is preserved and truncation related loss is minimized. The solution must scale for heavy workloads and work reliably across diverse document structures. As a GenAI developer, which approach would you recommend to address the content handling issue?
options: A) Use a semantic chunking strategy combined with static token limits per section and precomputed summaries for every chunk. Concatenate all summaries into a single prompt before model invocation and rely on truncation to discard excess tokens when limits are exceeded. Adjust chunk size thresholds periodically based on average document length.

B) Use a hierarchical chunking strategy that divides documents into fixed sections such as chapters, headings, and paragraphs. Aggregate child chunks into parent summaries and pass the top level summaries to the model. Increase chunk depth to reduce the chance of truncation during inference.

C) Use a semantic chunking strategy that splits documents based on meaning and topic boundaries before generating embeddings with Amazon Bedrock. Pass semantically coherent chunks to the model so each request fits within the context window. Preserve relevance by selecting chunks dynamically at query time.

D) Use fixed size token based chunking and rely on prompt compression techniques to reduce overall input length. Truncate lower priority chunks first when token limits are reached. Monitor truncation events using logging services to tune chunk sizes over time.
explanation: Truncation-related content loss in large-document processing is best addressed at the source — chunk boundaries that respect meaning, plus dynamic per-query selection so each model call only receives what's actually relevant and fits the context window. C) Semantic chunking splits on topic/meaning boundaries rather than arbitrary size, keeping each chunk coherent; generating embeddings enables dynamic, query-time selection of only the most relevant chunks, so each request naturally fits within context limits without truncation — this scales because selection adapts to the query, not the document's total size. A) Still concatenates ALL chunk summaries into a single prompt and relies on truncation to discard excess — this recreates the exact context-overflow problem the redesign is meant to solve, just with an extra summarization step first. B) Fixed hierarchical sectioning (chapters/headings/paragraphs) with parent-summary aggregation can strip critical query-specific details during summarization, and doesn't adapt to which content is actually relevant to a given question — increasing depth adds complexity without guaranteeing fit. D) Fixed-size token chunking ignores semantic boundaries and can split related information mid-thought; prompt compression can distort meaning, and heuristic truncation of 'lower priority' chunks doesn't reliably align with actual query relevance.

question: A global e-commerce company operates a conversational shopping assistant that helps customers discover products, understand return policies, and navigate catalog information across multiple Regions. Traffic analysis shows that customers frequently ask nearly identical questions with small wording variations, yet each request triggers a fresh model invocation, driving up token consumption and increasing operational costs. At the same time, users who are geographically distant from the primary hosting Region experience noticeably higher latency during peak shopping periods, especially during seasonal sales and major promotional events. As the lead GenAI architect, how should you implement a solution so that similar requests reuse prior results and frequent responses are served closer to end users? (Select two)
options: A) Store all user queries in Amazon DynamoDB and rely on exact string matching to determine whether a response can be reused. Enable API Gateway response caching to return previously computed answers only when the same request path is invoked.

B) Build a caching layer in Amazon OpenSearch Service that stores embeddings of entire product descriptions and use keyword boosted vector queries to retrieve potential matches before generating a new answer. Front the GenAI API with Amazon CloudFront so that cached API responses are returned when the same endpoint is accessed again.

C) Create an OpenSearch index that stores plain text versions of prompts and rely on keyword matching to identify potential cache hits. Front the API with CloudFront but set very short TTL values so that responses stay fresh for global users.

D) Build a semantic cache using Amazon OpenSearch Service to store embeddings of user queries and reuse prior responses when a new query is semantically similar. Place the GenAI API behind Amazon CloudFront so that frequently accessed responses are served from edge locations near end users.

E) Use Amazon Bedrock embeddings to compute vector representations of incoming questions and cache the resulting responses in Amazon ElastiCache for low latency retrieval. Configure CloudFront regional edge caches to serve popular API results globally, reducing latency across distant geographies.
explanation: Reusing responses across near-identical (but not identical) user phrasings needs a true semantic cache keyed on QUERY embeddings, paired with edge distribution for global latency — two valid backing-store implementations of the same core idea both qualify. D) A semantic cache embedding USER QUERIES (not product content) in OpenSearch correctly detects when differently-worded questions share the same intent, avoiding fresh model calls; CloudFront serves frequently-accessed responses from edge locations near distant users. E) Bedrock embeddings of incoming questions cached in ElastiCache achieves the same semantic-reuse goal with a different low-latency backing store; CloudFront regional edge caching again handles the geographic-latency half. A) Exact string matching misses all the near-duplicate phrasing variations the scenario describes, and API Gateway path-based caching doesn't vary by prompt CONTENT — wrong granularity entirely. B) Embedding PRODUCT DESCRIPTIONS instead of user queries doesn't detect when two different-phrased QUESTIONS share intent — this is catalog search, not conversational response caching; keyword-boosted vector queries also skew toward lexical rather than semantic similarity. C) Plain keyword matching on prompt text misses semantic similarity across differently-worded questions, and very-short CloudFront TTLs largely defeat the caching benefit for exactly the repeated queries the design is meant to capture.

task: 4.1 — Implement cost optimization and resource efficiency strategies
comparison_note: A different caching mechanism than AIPC01_D4_010's Bedrock native prompt caching — don't conflate the two. D4_010 caches a STATIC, UNCHANGED PREFIX (system instructions, citation rules) shared across many requests, reused via Bedrock's own CachePointBlock mechanism at the token level — it does nothing for varying user content. This question's semantic cache targets the opposite problem: DIFFERENT USERS asking DIFFERENTLY-WORDED but semantically equivalent full QUESTIONS — solved by embedding the queries themselves and doing similarity lookup, entirely outside Bedrock's native caching feature. If the shared content is a fixed instructional prefix → Bedrock prompt caching (D4_010); if the shared content is semantically-similar-but-differently-worded user questions → an application-level semantic cache (this pattern).

question: A ride sharing company is developing a Driver Risk Assistant that evaluates structured telemetry data, such as speed readings, acceleration patterns, braking events, and categorical driver ratings, to generate short natural language risk insights. The system should need minimum infrastructure management and must respond in under 400 milliseconds as well as scale to millions of requests per day while ensuring very low inference cost. It must also minimize hallucinations because risk insights feed into regulatory reporting and insurance calculations. The output must follow a strict JSON schema so that downstream safety analytics systems can reliably parse and aggregate the results. Which solution should the architect choose to meet all these requirements?
options: A) Use an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base to embed telemetry events and perform semantic searches for similar historical driving patterns, then generate a risk summary using a Titan text model. Aggregate retrieved examples and form the final structured JSON output from the model response.

B) Deploy a large fine tuned transformer model on Amazon SageMaker GPU instances and scale it with automatic instance count adjustments. Train the model specifically on telemetry data to improve risk reasoning accuracy while maintaining a consistent schema through custom post processing code in the inference container.

C) Use a Claude 3 Sonnet configuration to generate risk insights, and rely on prompt engineering to enforce schema rules. Adjust temperature and top p values to reduce hallucinations and improve consistency across high traffic scenarios.

D) Use a Titan Text Lite model configured with JSON mode or function calling so that outputs follow a predefined schema, and integrate response streaming via Amazon Bedrock Converse API to reduce token first latency.
explanation: Sub-400ms latency at millions-of-requests scale, guaranteed schema conformance (not just prompt-requested), and minimal infrastructure ownership together rule out large reasoning models, custom-hosted models, and semantic retrieval — and point to the smallest capable managed model with JSON mode. D) Titan Text Lite is built for low-latency, low-cost inference — a fit for short structured-input tasks at massive scale; JSON mode/function calling GUARANTEES schema-conforming output (not just prompt-requested formatting), eliminating fragile downstream parsing logic; Converse API streaming further reduces time-to-first-token. A) Telemetry (numeric readings, timestamps, categorical values) isn't a good match for semantic embedding/retrieval at all, and adding a Knowledge Base retrieval step introduces latency that would violate the sub-400ms requirement. B) A custom fine-tuned model on SageMaker GPU instances requires managing instances, autoscaling, container logic, and custom schema-enforcement code — real infrastructure ownership the requirement explicitly wants minimized, plus added cost/latency overhead. C) Claude 3 Sonnet is a larger, higher-latency, higher-cost model — a poor fit for a strict sub-400ms budget at massive scale, and relying on prompt engineering ALONE (no JSON mode/function calling) doesn't guarantee schema correctness — structural accuracy remains variable.
